questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem:
Which of the following statements are true?

I. Any $2\times 3$ matrix $A$ has at most $2$ distinct singular values.

II. The matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}]$ has one negative singular value.

III. Any $5\times 3$ matrix $A$ has at most $3$ distinct singular values.
questions.worked_solution:
The singular values of the matrix $A$ are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix ${A}^{T}\,A.$ 

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is false. Since $A$ is a $2\times 3$ matrix and ${A}^{T}$ is a $3\times 2$ matrix, ${A}^{T}\,A$ must be a $3\times 3$ matrix: 

$$
{{A}^{T}}_{3\times 2}\times {A}_{2\times 3}={{A}^{T}\,A}_{3\times 3}
$$

Hence, $A$ has at most $3$ distinct singular values.

- Statement II is false. All singular values of any matrix are non-negative. So, $A$ can't have a negative singular value.

- Statement III is true. Since $A$ is a $5\times 3$ matrix and ${A}^{T}$ is a $3\times 5$ matrix, ${A}^{T}\,A$ must be a $3\times 3$ matrix: 

$$
{{A}^{T}}_{3\times 5}\times {A}_{5\times 3}={{A}^{T}\,A}_{3\times 3}
$$

Hence, $A$ has at most $3$ distinct singular values.

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only."

questions.name: Question 2
questions.problem:
Which of the following statements are true?

I. Any $4\times 2$ matrix $A$ has at most $2$ distinct singular values.

II. Any matrix of the form  $A=[\begin{aligned}-a & 0 \\ 0 & a\end{aligned}]$ has exactly one negative and one positive singular value.

III. Any $2\times 4$ matrix $A$ has at most $4$ distinct singular values.
questions.worked_solution:
The singular values of the matrix $A$ are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix ${A}^{T}\,A.$ 

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is true. Since $A$ is a $4\times 2$ matrix and ${A}^{T}$ is a $2\times 4$ matrix, ${A}^{T}\,A$ must be a $2\times 2$ matrix: 

$$
{{A}^{T}}_{2\times 4}\times {A}_{4\times 2}={{A}^{T}\,A}_{2\times 2}
$$

Hence, $A$ has at most $2$ distinct singular values.

- Statement II is false.  All singular values of any matrix are non-negative. So, 
$A$  can't have any negative singular value.

- Statement III is true.  Indeed,  since $A$ is a $2\times 4$ matrix and ${A}^{T}$ is a $4\times 2$ matrix, ${A}^{T}\,A$ must be a $4\times 4$ matrix: 

$$
{{A}^{T}}_{4\times 2}\times {A}_{2\times 4}={{A}^{T}\,A}_{4\times 4}
$$

Hence, $A$ has at most $4$ distinct singular values.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only."

questions.name: Question 3
questions.problem: What are the singular values of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & -2 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 2\end{aligned}]?$
questions.worked_solution:
The singular values of the matrix $A$ are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix ${A}^{T}\,A.$ 

First, we calculate ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & -2 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 2\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & -2 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & -1 \\ -2 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & -2 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 5 & -2 \\ 0 & -2 & 8\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the characteristic equation of ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|{A}^{T}\,A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}0-\lambda  & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 5-\lambda  & -2 \\ 0 & -2 & 8-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-\lambda )|\begin{aligned}5-\lambda  & -2 \\ -2 & 8-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-\lambda )((5-\lambda )(8-\lambda )-4) & =0 \\ (-\lambda )({\lambda }^{2}-13\lambda +36) & =0 \\ -\lambda (\lambda -4)(\lambda -9) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =9,\,4,\,0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the singular values of $A$ are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }_{1} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{1}}=\sqrt{9}=3 \\ {\sigma }_{2} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{2}}=\sqrt{4}=2 \\ {\sigma }_{3} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{3}}=\sqrt{0}=0\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 4
questions.problem: What are the singular values of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}4 & -1 \\ 1 & -4\end{aligned}]?$
questions.worked_solution:
The singular values of the matrix $A$ are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix ${A}^{T}\,A.$ 

First, we calculate ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={[\begin{aligned}4 & -1 \\ 1 & -4\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}4 & -1 \\ 1 & -4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 1 \\ -1 & -4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}4 & -1 \\ 1 & -4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}17 & -8 \\ -8 & 17\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the characteristic equation of ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|{A}^{T}\,A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}17-\lambda  & -8 \\ -8 & 17-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (17-\lambda )(17-\lambda )-64 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-34\lambda +289-64 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-34\lambda +225 & =0 \\ (\lambda -9)(\lambda -25) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =25,\,9\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the singular values of $A$ are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }_{1} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{1}}=\sqrt{25}=5 \\ {\sigma }_{2} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{2}}=\sqrt{9}=3\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 5
questions.problem: What are the singular values of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 0\end{aligned}]?$
questions.worked_solution:
The singular values of the matrix $A$ are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix ${A}^{T}\,A.$ 

First, we calculate ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 0\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 0 \\ 2 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the characteristic equation of ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|{A}^{T}\,A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & 2 & 0 \\ 2 & 4-\lambda  & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ -\lambda |\begin{aligned}4-\lambda  & 2 \\ 2 & 1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ -\lambda [(1-\lambda )(4-\lambda )-4)] & =0 \\ -\lambda ({\lambda }^{2}-5\lambda +4-4) & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}(\lambda -5) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =5,\,0,\,0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the singular values of $A$ are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }_{1} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{1}}=\sqrt{5} \\ {\sigma }_{2} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{2}}=\sqrt{0}=0 \\ {\sigma }_{3} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{3}}=\sqrt{0}=0\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 6
questions.problem: What are the singular values of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}\,0 & \,1 \\ \,\,-2 & \,\,-2 \\ \,\,-1 & 0\end{aligned}]?$
questions.worked_solution:
The singular values of the matrix $A$ are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix ${A}^{T}\,A.$ 

First, we calculate ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={[\begin{aligned}\,0 & \,1 \\ \,\,-2 & \,\,-2 \\ \,\,-1 & 0\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}\,0 & \,1 \\ \,\,-2 & \,\,-2 \\ \,\,-1 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 & -1 \\ 1 & -2 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}\,0 & \,1 \\ \,\,-2 & \,\,-2 \\ \,\,-1 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}5 & 4 \\ 4 & 5\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the characteristic equation of ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|{A}^{T}\,A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}5-\lambda  & 4 \\ 4 & 5-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (5-\lambda )(5-\lambda )-16 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-10\lambda +25-16 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-10\lambda +9 & =0 \\ (\lambda -9)(\lambda -1) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =9,\,1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the singular values of $A$ are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }_{1} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{1}}=\sqrt{9}=3 \\ {\sigma }_{2} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{2}}=\sqrt{1}=1\end{aligned}
$$

Example: 
                    Identifying True Statements Regarding the Singular Values of a Matrix
canonical_examples.problem:
Which of the following statements are true?

I. Any $1\times4$ matrix $A$ has at most $1$ singular value.

II. Any $4\times2$ matrix $A$ has at most $2$ distinct singular values.

III. The matrix ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14180034/assets/b8601b1e66ef1d302e7194f262f6a513063bba2114fb063c2fc16542d4684392.svg) has one negative singular value.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The singular values of the matrix $A$ are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix $A^T \! A.$ 

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is false. Since $A$ is a $1 \times 4$ matrix and $A^T$ is a $4\times 1$ matrix, $A^T \! A$ must be a $4 \times 4$ matrix: 

$$
\underset{\bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 4} \times {\large 1}}{A^T} \times \underset{{\large 1} \times \bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 4}}{A} =  
\underset{\bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 4} \times \bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 4}}{A^T \! A}
$$

Hence, $A$ has at most $4$ distinct singular values.

- Statement II is true. Since $A$ is a $4 \times 2$ matrix and $A^T$ is a $2\times 4$ matrix, $A^T \! A$ must be a $2 \times 2$ matrix: 

$$
\underset{\bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 2} \times {\large 4}}{A^T} \times \underset{{\large 4} \times \bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 2}}{A} = 
\underset{\bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 2} \times \bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 2}}{A^T \! A}
$$

Hence, $A$ has at most $2$ distinct singular values.

- Statement III is false. All singular values of any matrix are non-negative. So, $A$ cannot have a negative singular value.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."

canonical_examples.problem: What are the singular values of the matrix ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14180034/assets/590d5dc32950efa0fce63a5d64a5595210a3ccb08c613e364586dba4822d7314.svg)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The singular values of the matrix $A$ are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix $A^T \! A.$  

First, we calculate $A^T \! A\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the characteristic equation of $A^T \! A\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}|{A}^{T}\,A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1-\lambda  & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )|\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & 0 \\ 0 & 1-\lambda \end{aligned}|+|\begin{aligned}0 & 1-\lambda  \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )(1-\lambda )^{2}-(1-\lambda ) & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )((1-\lambda )^{2}-1) & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )({\lambda }^{2}-2\lambda ) & =0 \\ -\lambda (\lambda -1)(\lambda -2) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =2,\,1,\,0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the singular values of $A$ are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }_{1} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{1}}=\sqrt{2} \\ {\sigma }_{2} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{2}}=\sqrt{1}=1 \\ {\sigma }_{3} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{3}}=\sqrt{0}=0\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding the Singular Values of a Rectangular Matrix

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
Recall that the singular values of a real matrix $A$ are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix $A^T \! A.$

Also, since $A^T \! A$ is a positive semi-definite matrix, the eigenvalues of $A^T \! A$ must be always non-negative real numbers.

Let's compute the singular values of the matrix $A,$ given by 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14180034/assets/a9edbe1fee59758c9557d95ea8f62468f9f3cb98449c437a274bdbf5c30f7dc6.svg)

Now, since

- $A$ is a $3 \times 2$ matrix, and

- $A^T$ is a $2 \times 3$ matrix,

then $A^T \! A$  must be a $2 \times 2$ matrix:

$$
\underset{\bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 2} \times {\large 3}}{A^T} \times \underset{{\large 3} \times \bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 2}}{A} = 
\underset{\bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 2} \times \bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 2}}{A^T \! A}
$$

Let's now compute our singular values. First, we calculate $A^T \! A\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={[\begin{aligned}\,0 & \,2 \\ \,\,-2 & \,0 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}\,0 & \,2 \\ \,\,-2 & \,0 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 & 2 \\ 2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}\,0 & \,2 \\ \,\,-2 & \,0 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}8 & 2 \\ 2 & 5\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we compute the eigenvalues of $A^T \! A\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}|{A}^{T}\,A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}8-\lambda  & 2 \\ 2 & 5-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (8-\lambda )(5-\lambda )-4 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-13\lambda +36 & =0 \\ (\lambda -9)(\lambda -4) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =9,\,4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the singular values of $A$ are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }_{1} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{1}}=\sqrt{9}=3 \\ {\sigma }_{2} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{2}}=\sqrt{4}=2\end{aligned}
$$

Note the following:

- When listing the singular values of a matrix, we usually write them in descending order.

- If $A$ is a $m\times n$ matrix, then $A^T A$ is a $n\times n$ positive semi-definite matrix. This means that $A$ has *at most* $n$ distinct singular values.

tutorials.content:
Recall that the singular values of a real matrix $A$ are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix $A^T \! A.$

Also, since $A^T \! A$ is a positive semi-definite matrix, the eigenvalues of $A^T \! A$ must be always non-negative real numbers.

Let's compute the singular values of the matrix $A,$ given by 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14180034/assets/a9edbe1fee59758c9557d95ea8f62468f9f3cb98449c437a274bdbf5c30f7dc6.svg)

Now, since

- $A$ is a $3 \times 2$ matrix, and

- $A^T$ is a $2 \times 3$ matrix,

then $A^T \! A$  must be a $2 \times 2$ matrix:

$$
\underset{\bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 2} \times {\large 3}}{A^T} \times \underset{{\large 3} \times \bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 2}}{A} = 
\underset{\bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 2} \times \bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 2}}{A^T \! A}
$$

Let's now compute our singular values. First, we calculate $A^T \! A\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={[\begin{aligned}\,0 & \,2 \\ \,\,-2 & \,0 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}\,0 & \,2 \\ \,\,-2 & \,0 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 & 2 \\ 2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}\,0 & \,2 \\ \,\,-2 & \,0 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}8 & 2 \\ 2 & 5\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we compute the eigenvalues of $A^T \! A\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}|{A}^{T}\,A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}8-\lambda  & 2 \\ 2 & 5-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (8-\lambda )(5-\lambda )-4 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-13\lambda +36 & =0 \\ (\lambda -9)(\lambda -4) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =9,\,4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the singular values of $A$ are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }_{1} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{1}}=\sqrt{9}=3 \\ {\sigma }_{2} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{2}}=\sqrt{4}=2\end{aligned}
$$

Note the following:

- When listing the singular values of a matrix, we usually write them in descending order.

- If $A$ is a $m\times n$ matrix, then $A^T A$ is a $n\times n$ positive semi-definite matrix. This means that $A$ has *at most* $n$ distinct singular values.

tutorial.content:
Recall that the singular values of a real matrix $A$ are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix $A^T \! A.$

Also, since $A^T \! A$ is a positive semi-definite matrix, the eigenvalues of $A^T \! A$ must be always non-negative real numbers.

Let's compute the singular values of the matrix $A,$ given by 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14180034/assets/27384e999cf503b9c0f827f81fca7ad68451b351edaab53187918687e101e011.svg)

Now, since

- $A$ is a $3 \times 2$ matrix, and

- $A^T$ is a $2 \times 3$ matrix,

then $A^T \! A$  must be a $2 \times 2$ matrix:

$$
\underset{\bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 2} \times {\large 3}}{A^T} \times \underset{{\large 3} \times \bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 2}}{A} = 
\underset{\bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 2} \times \bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 2}}{A^T \! A}
$$

Let's now compute our singular values. First, we calculate $A^T \! A\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={[\begin{aligned}\,0 & \,2 \\ \,\,-2 & \,0 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}\,0 & \,2 \\ \,\,-2 & \,0 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 & 2 \\ 2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}\,0 & \,2 \\ \,\,-2 & \,0 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}8 & 2 \\ 2 & 5\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we compute the eigenvalues of $A^T \! A\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}|{A}^{T}\,A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}8-\lambda  & 2 \\ 2 & 5-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (8-\lambda )(5-\lambda )-4 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-13\lambda +36 & =0 \\ (\lambda -9)(\lambda -4) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =9,\,4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the singular values of $A$ are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }_{1} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{1}}=\sqrt{9}=3 \\ {\sigma }_{2} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{2}}=\sqrt{4}=2\end{aligned}
$$

Note the following:

- When listing the singular values of a matrix, we usually write them in descending order.

- If $A$ is a $m\times n$ matrix, then $A^T A$ is a $n\times n$ positive semi-definite matrix. This means that $A$ has *at most* $n$ distinct singular values.

The singular values of the matrix $A$ are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix $A^T \! A.$ 

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is false. Since $A$ is a $1 \times 4$ matrix and $A^T$ is a $4\times 1$ matrix, $A^T \! A$ must be a $4 \times 4$ matrix: 

$$
\underset{\bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 4} \times {\large 1}}{A^T} \times \underset{{\large 1} \times \bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 4}}{A} =  
\underset{\bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 4} \times \bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 4}}{A^T \! A}
$$

Hence, $A$ has at most $4$ distinct singular values.

- Statement II is true. Since $A$ is a $4 \times 2$ matrix and $A^T$ is a $2\times 4$ matrix, $A^T \! A$ must be a $2 \times 2$ matrix: 

$$
\underset{\bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 2} \times {\large 4}}{A^T} \times \underset{{\large 4} \times \bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 2}}{A} = 
\underset{\bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 2} \times \bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 2}}{A^T \! A}
$$

Hence, $A$ has at most $2$ distinct singular values.

- Statement III is false. All singular values of any matrix are non-negative. So, $A$ cannot have a negative singular value.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."

observed_steps.name: Example: Finding the Singular Values of a Square Matrix
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Identifying True Statements Regarding the Singular Values of a Matrix
observed_steps.worked_solution:
The singular values of the matrix $A$ are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix $A^T \! A.$  

First, we calculate $A^T \! A\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}5 & 4 \\ 4 & 5\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the characteristic equation of $A^T \! A\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}|{A}^{T}\,A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}5-\lambda  & 4 \\ 4 & 5-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (5-\lambda )^{2}-16 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-10\lambda +9 & =0 \\ (\lambda -1)(\lambda -9) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =9,\,1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the singular values of $A$ are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }_{1} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{1}}=\sqrt{9}=3 \\ {\sigma }_{2} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{2}}=\sqrt{1}=1\end{aligned}
$$

observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Finding the Singular Values of a Square Matrix
observed_steps.worked_solution:
The singular values of the matrix $A$ are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix ${A}^{T}\,A.$ 

First, we calculate ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & -2 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 2\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & -2 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & -1 \\ -2 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & -2 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 5 & -2 \\ 0 & -2 & 8\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the characteristic equation of ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|{A}^{T}\,A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}0-\lambda  & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 5-\lambda  & -2 \\ 0 & -2 & 8-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-\lambda )|\begin{aligned}5-\lambda  & -2 \\ -2 & 8-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-\lambda )((5-\lambda )(8-\lambda )-4) & =0 \\ (-\lambda )({\lambda }^{2}-13\lambda +36) & =0 \\ -\lambda (\lambda -4)(\lambda -9) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =9,\,4,\,0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the singular values of $A$ are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }_{1} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{1}}=\sqrt{9}=3 \\ {\sigma }_{2} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{2}}=\sqrt{4}=2 \\ {\sigma }_{3} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{3}}=\sqrt{0}=0\end{aligned}
$$

b

c

The singular values of the matrix A are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix ATA.

First, we calculate ATA:

ATA=[00−20200−12]T[00−20200−12]=[00002−1−202][00−20200−12]=[00005−20−28]

Now, we solve the characteristic equation of ATA:

|ATA−λI|=0|0−λ0005−λ−20−28−λ|=0(−λ)|5−λ−2−28−λ|=0(−λ)((5−λ)(8−λ)−4)=0(−λ)(λ2−13λ+36)=0−λ(λ−4)(λ−9)=0λ=9,4,0

observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Finding the Singular Values of a Square Matrix
observed_steps.worked_solution:
The singular values of the matrix $A$ are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix ${A}^{T}\,A.$ 

First, we calculate ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={[\begin{aligned}4 & -1 \\ 1 & -4\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}4 & -1 \\ 1 & -4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 1 \\ -1 & -4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}4 & -1 \\ 1 & -4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}17 & -8 \\ -8 & 17\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the characteristic equation of ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|{A}^{T}\,A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}17-\lambda  & -8 \\ -8 & 17-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (17-\lambda )(17-\lambda )-64 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-34\lambda +289-64 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-34\lambda +225 & =0 \\ (\lambda -9)(\lambda -25) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =25,\,9\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the singular values of $A$ are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }_{1} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{1}}=\sqrt{25}=5 \\ {\sigma }_{2} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{2}}=\sqrt{9}=3\end{aligned}
$$

Question 4
?

What are the singular values of the matrix A=[4−11−4]?

a
16 and 4
b
5 and 3
c
3 and 2
d
8 and 4
e
25 and 9
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The singular values of the matrix A are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix ATA.

First, we calculate ATA:

ATA=[4−11−4]T[4−11−4]=[41−1−4][4−11−4]=[17−8−817]

Now, we solve the characteristic equation of ATA:

|ATA−λI|=0|17−λ−8−817−λ|=0(17−λ)(17−λ)−64=0λ2−34λ+289−64=0λ2−34λ+225=0(λ−9)(λ−25)=0λ=25,9

Therefore, the singular values of A are as follows:

σ1=λ1=25=5σ2=λ2=9=3

observed_steps.worked_solution:
The singular values of the matrix $A$ are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix $A^T \! A.$  

First, we calculate $A^T \! A\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the characteristic equation of $A^T \! A\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}|{A}^{T}\,A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1-\lambda  & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )|\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & 0 \\ 0 & 1-\lambda \end{aligned}|+|\begin{aligned}0 & 1-\lambda  \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )(1-\lambda )^{2}-(1-\lambda ) & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )((1-\lambda )^{2}-1) & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )({\lambda }^{2}-2\lambda ) & =0 \\ -\lambda (\lambda -1)(\lambda -2) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =2,\,1,\,0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the singular values of $A$ are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }_{1} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{1}}=\sqrt{2} \\ {\sigma }_{2} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{2}}=\sqrt{1}=1 \\ {\sigma }_{3} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{3}}=\sqrt{0}=0\end{aligned}
$$

observed_steps.worked_solution:
The singular values of the matrix $A$ are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix ${A}^{T}\,A.$ 

First, we calculate ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 0\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 0 \\ 2 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the characteristic equation of ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|{A}^{T}\,A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & 2 & 0 \\ 2 & 4-\lambda  & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ -\lambda |\begin{aligned}4-\lambda  & 2 \\ 2 & 1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ -\lambda [(1-\lambda )(4-\lambda )-4)] & =0 \\ -\lambda ({\lambda }^{2}-5\lambda +4-4) & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}(\lambda -5) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =5,\,0,\,0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the singular values of $A$ are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }_{1} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{1}}=\sqrt{5} \\ {\sigma }_{2} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{2}}=\sqrt{0}=0 \\ {\sigma }_{3} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{3}}=\sqrt{0}=0\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the characteristic equation of ATA:

observed_steps.name: Question 6
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Finding the Singular Values of a Rectangular Matrix
observed_steps.worked_solution:
The singular values of the matrix $A$ are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix ${A}^{T}\,A.$ 

First, we calculate ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={[\begin{aligned}\,0 & \,1 \\ \,\,-2 & \,\,-2 \\ \,\,-1 & 0\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}\,0 & \,1 \\ \,\,-2 & \,\,-2 \\ \,\,-1 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 & -1 \\ 1 & -2 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}\,0 & \,1 \\ \,\,-2 & \,\,-2 \\ \,\,-1 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}5 & 4 \\ 4 & 5\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the characteristic equation of ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|{A}^{T}\,A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}5-\lambda  & 4 \\ 4 & 5-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (5-\lambda )(5-\lambda )-16 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-10\lambda +25-16 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-10\lambda +9 & =0 \\ (\lambda -9)(\lambda -1) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =9,\,1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the singular values of $A$ are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }_{1} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{1}}=\sqrt{9}=3 \\ {\sigma }_{2} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{2}}=\sqrt{1}=1\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }_{1} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{1}}=\sqrt{9}=3 \\ {\sigma }_{2} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{2}}=\sqrt{1}=1\end{aligned}

question.name: Question 1
question.problem:
Which of the following statements are true?

I. Any $2\times 3$ matrix $A$ has at most $2$ distinct singular values.

II. The matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}]$ has one negative singular value.

III. Any $5\times 3$ matrix $A$ has at most $3$ distinct singular values.
question.worked_solution:
The singular values of the matrix $A$ are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix ${A}^{T}\,A.$ 

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is false. Since $A$ is a $2\times 3$ matrix and ${A}^{T}$ is a $3\times 2$ matrix, ${A}^{T}\,A$ must be a $3\times 3$ matrix: 

$$
{{A}^{T}}_{3\times 2}\times {A}_{2\times 3}={{A}^{T}\,A}_{3\times 3}
$$

Hence, $A$ has at most $3$ distinct singular values.

- Statement II is false. All singular values of any matrix are non-negative. So, $A$ can't have a negative singular value.

- Statement III is true. Since $A$ is a $5\times 3$ matrix and ${A}^{T}$ is a $3\times 5$ matrix, ${A}^{T}\,A$ must be a $3\times 3$ matrix: 

$$
{{A}^{T}}_{3\times 5}\times {A}_{5\times 3}={{A}^{T}\,A}_{3\times 3}
$$

Hence, $A$ has at most $3$ distinct singular values.

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only."

$$

- Statement II is false. All singular values of any matrix are non-negative. So, $A$ can't have a negative singular value.

- Statement III is true. Since $A$ is a $5\times 3$ matrix and ${A}^{T}$ is a $3\times 5$ matrix, ${A}^{T}\,A$ must be a $3\times 3$ matrix: 

$$
{{A}^{T}}_{3\times 5}\times {A}_{5\times 3}={{A}^{T}\,A}_{3\times 3}
$$

Hence, $A$ has at most $3$ distinct singular values.

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only."

question.name: Question 3
question.problem: What are the singular values of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & -2 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 2\end{aligned}]?$
question.worked_solution:
The singular values of the matrix $A$ are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix ${A}^{T}\,A.$ 

First, we calculate ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & -2 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 2\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & -2 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & -1 \\ -2 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & -2 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 5 & -2 \\ 0 & -2 & 8\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the characteristic equation of ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|{A}^{T}\,A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}0-\lambda  & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 5-\lambda  & -2 \\ 0 & -2 & 8-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-\lambda )|\begin{aligned}5-\lambda  & -2 \\ -2 & 8-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-\lambda )((5-\lambda )(8-\lambda )-4) & =0 \\ (-\lambda )({\lambda }^{2}-13\lambda +36) & =0 \\ -\lambda (\lambda -4)(\lambda -9) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =9,\,4,\,0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the singular values of $A$ are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }_{1} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{1}}=\sqrt{9}=3 \\ {\sigma }_{2} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{2}}=\sqrt{4}=2 \\ {\sigma }_{3} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{3}}=\sqrt{0}=0\end{aligned}
$$

last_observation.name: Question 3
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Finding the Singular Values of a Square Matrix
last_observation.worked_solution:
The singular values of the matrix $A$ are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix ${A}^{T}\,A.$ 

First, we calculate ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & -2 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 2\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & -2 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & -1 \\ -2 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & -2 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 5 & -2 \\ 0 & -2 & 8\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the characteristic equation of ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|{A}^{T}\,A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}0-\lambda  & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 5-\lambda  & -2 \\ 0 & -2 & 8-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-\lambda )|\begin{aligned}5-\lambda  & -2 \\ -2 & 8-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-\lambda )((5-\lambda )(8-\lambda )-4) & =0 \\ (-\lambda )({\lambda }^{2}-13\lambda +36) & =0 \\ -\lambda (\lambda -4)(\lambda -9) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =9,\,4,\,0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the singular values of $A$ are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }_{1} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{1}}=\sqrt{9}=3 \\ {\sigma }_{2} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{2}}=\sqrt{4}=2 \\ {\sigma }_{3} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{3}}=\sqrt{0}=0\end{aligned}
$$

Question 3
?

What are the singular values of the matrix A=[00−20200−12]?

a
3,2,0
b
5,2,1
c
2,2,0
d
4,1,0
e
9,4,0
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The singular values of the matrix A are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix ATA.

First, we calculate ATA:

ATA=[00−20200−12]T[00−20200−12]=[00002−1−202][00−20200−12]=[00005−20−28]

Now, we solve the characteristic equation of ATA:

|ATA−λI|=0|0−λ0005−λ−20−28−λ|=0(−λ)|5−λ−2−28−λ|=0(−λ)((5−λ)(8−λ)−4)=0(−λ)(λ2−13λ+36)=0−λ(λ−4)(λ−9)=0λ=9,4,0

Therefore, the singular values of A are as follows:

σ1=λ1=9=3σ2=λ2=4=2σ3=λ3=0=0

solution.reasoning: A^T A has rows (0,0,0), (0,5,-2), and (0,-2,8). Its characteristic polynomial is -λ(λ²-13λ+36)=-λ(λ-9)(λ-4), so its eigenvalues are 9, 4, and 0. Their nonnegative square roots are 3, 2, and 0, giving option a. No answer or grade for the current question is captured.

question.name: Question 4
question.problem: What are the singular values of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}4 & -1 \\ 1 & -4\end{aligned}]?$
question.worked_solution:
The singular values of the matrix $A$ are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix ${A}^{T}\,A.$ 

First, we calculate ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={[\begin{aligned}4 & -1 \\ 1 & -4\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}4 & -1 \\ 1 & -4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 1 \\ -1 & -4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}4 & -1 \\ 1 & -4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}17 & -8 \\ -8 & 17\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the characteristic equation of ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|{A}^{T}\,A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}17-\lambda  & -8 \\ -8 & 17-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (17-\lambda )(17-\lambda )-64 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-34\lambda +289-64 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-34\lambda +225 & =0 \\ (\lambda -9)(\lambda -25) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =25,\,9\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the singular values of $A$ are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }_{1} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{1}}=\sqrt{25}=5 \\ {\sigma }_{2} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{2}}=\sqrt{9}=3\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 4
?

What are the singular values of the matrix A=[4−11−4]?

a
16 and 4
b
5 and 3
c
3 and 2
d
8 and 4
e
25 and 9
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The singular values of the matrix A are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix ATA.

First, we calculate ATA:

ATA=[4−11−4]T[4−11−4]=[41−1−4][4−11−4]=[17−8−817]

Now, we solve the characteristic equation of ATA:

|ATA−λI|=0|17−λ−8−817−λ|=0(17−λ)(17−λ)−64=0λ2−34λ+289−64=0λ2−34λ+225=0(λ−9)(λ−25)=0λ=25,9

Therefore, the singular values of A are as follows:

σ1=λ1=25=5σ2=λ2=9=3
question.knowledge_point: Finding the Singular Values of a Square Matrix

solution.reasoning: A^T A=[[17,-8],[-8,17]] has eigenvalues 25 and 9. The singular values are their nonnegative square roots, 5 and 3, so choose b. No current-question answer or grade is captured.

feedback.name: Question 4
feedback.problem: What are the singular values of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}4 & -1 \\ 1 & -4\end{aligned}]?$
feedback.worked_solution:
The singular values of the matrix $A$ are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix ${A}^{T}\,A.$ 

First, we calculate ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={[\begin{aligned}4 & -1 \\ 1 & -4\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}4 & -1 \\ 1 & -4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 1 \\ -1 & -4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}4 & -1 \\ 1 & -4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}17 & -8 \\ -8 & 17\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the characteristic equation of ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|{A}^{T}\,A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}17-\lambda  & -8 \\ -8 & 17-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (17-\lambda )(17-\lambda )-64 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-34\lambda +289-64 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-34\lambda +225 & =0 \\ (\lambda -9)(\lambda -25) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =25,\,9\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the singular values of $A$ are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }_{1} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{1}}=\sqrt{25}=5 \\ {\sigma }_{2} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{2}}=\sqrt{9}=3\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 5
question.problem: What are the singular values of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 0\end{aligned}]?$
question.worked_solution:
The singular values of the matrix $A$ are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix ${A}^{T}\,A.$ 

First, we calculate ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 0\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 0 \\ 2 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the characteristic equation of ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|{A}^{T}\,A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & 2 & 0 \\ 2 & 4-\lambda  & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ -\lambda |\begin{aligned}4-\lambda  & 2 \\ 2 & 1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ -\lambda [(1-\lambda )(4-\lambda )-4)] & =0 \\ -\lambda ({\lambda }^{2}-5\lambda +4-4) & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}(\lambda -5) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =5,\,0,\,0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the singular values of $A$ are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }_{1} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{1}}=\sqrt{5} \\ {\sigma }_{2} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{2}}=\sqrt{0}=0 \\ {\sigma }_{3} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{3}}=\sqrt{0}=0\end{aligned}
$$

5,5,0

Correct

ATA=[120]T[120]=[120][120]=[120240000]

|ATA−λI|=0|1−λ2024−λ000−λ|=0−λ|4−λ221−λ|=0−λ[(1−λ)(4−λ)−4)]=0−λ(λ2−5λ+4−4)=0λ2(λ−5)=0λ=5,0,0

σ1=λ1=5σ2=λ2=0=0σ3=λ3=0=0

last_observation.name: Question 5
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Finding the Singular Values of a Rectangular Matrix
last_observation.worked_solution:
The singular values of the matrix $A$ are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix ${A}^{T}\,A.$ 

First, we calculate ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 0\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 0 \\ 2 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the characteristic equation of ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|{A}^{T}\,A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & 2 & 0 \\ 2 & 4-\lambda  & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ -\lambda |\begin{aligned}4-\lambda  & 2 \\ 2 & 1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ -\lambda [(1-\lambda )(4-\lambda )-4)] & =0 \\ -\lambda ({\lambda }^{2}-5\lambda +4-4) & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}(\lambda -5) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =5,\,0,\,0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the singular values of $A$ are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }_{1} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{1}}=\sqrt{5} \\ {\sigma }_{2} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{2}}=\sqrt{0}=0 \\ {\sigma }_{3} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{3}}=\sqrt{0}=0\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 5
?

What are the singular values of the matrix A=[120]?

a
25,5,0
b
5,0,0
c
5,0,0
d
5,5,0
e
5,1,0
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The singular values of the matrix A are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix ATA.

First, we calculate ATA:

ATA=[120]T[120]=[120][120]=[120240000]

Now, we solve the characteristic equation of ATA:

|ATA−λI|=0|1−λ2024−λ000−λ|=0−λ|4−λ221−λ|=0−λ[(1−λ)(4−λ)−4)]=0−λ(λ2−5λ+4−4)=0λ2(λ−5)=0λ=5,0,0

Therefore, the singular values of A are as follows:

σ1=λ1=5σ2=λ2=0=0σ3=λ3=0=0

question.name: Question 6
question.problem: What are the singular values of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}\,0 & \,1 \\ \,\,-2 & \,\,-2 \\ \,\,-1 & 0\end{aligned}]?$
question.worked_solution:
The singular values of the matrix $A$ are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix ${A}^{T}\,A.$ 

First, we calculate ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={[\begin{aligned}\,0 & \,1 \\ \,\,-2 & \,\,-2 \\ \,\,-1 & 0\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}\,0 & \,1 \\ \,\,-2 & \,\,-2 \\ \,\,-1 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 & -1 \\ 1 & -2 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}\,0 & \,1 \\ \,\,-2 & \,\,-2 \\ \,\,-1 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}5 & 4 \\ 4 & 5\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the characteristic equation of ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|{A}^{T}\,A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}5-\lambda  & 4 \\ 4 & 5-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (5-\lambda )(5-\lambda )-16 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-10\lambda +25-16 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-10\lambda +9 & =0 \\ (\lambda -9)(\lambda -1) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =9,\,1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the singular values of $A$ are as follows:

$$

question.html:
Question 6
?

What are the singular values of the matrix A=[01−2−2−10]?

a
3 and 1
b
9 and 1
c
12 and 9
d
3 and 2
e
2 and 1
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The singular values of the matrix A are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix ATA.

First, we calculate ATA:

ATA=[01−2−2−10]T[01−2−2−10]=[0−2−11−20][01−2−2−10]=[5445]

Now, we solve the characteristic equation of ATA:

|ATA−λI|=0|5−λ445−λ|=0(5−λ)(5−λ)−16=0λ2−10λ+25−16=0λ2−10λ+9=0(λ−9)(λ−1)=0λ=9,1

Therefore, the singular values of A are as follows:

σ1=λ1=9=3σ2=λ2=1=1

last_observation.worked_solution:
The singular values of the matrix $A$ are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix ${A}^{T}\,A.$ 

First, we calculate ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={[\begin{aligned}\,0 & \,1 \\ \,\,-2 & \,\,-2 \\ \,\,-1 & 0\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}\,0 & \,1 \\ \,\,-2 & \,\,-2 \\ \,\,-1 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 & -1 \\ 1 & -2 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}\,0 & \,1 \\ \,\,-2 & \,\,-2 \\ \,\,-1 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}5 & 4 \\ 4 & 5\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the characteristic equation of ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|{A}^{T}\,A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}5-\lambda  & 4 \\ 4 & 5-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (5-\lambda )(5-\lambda )-16 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-10\lambda +25-16 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-10\lambda +9 & =0 \\ (\lambda -9)(\lambda -1) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =9,\,1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the singular values of $A$ are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }_{1} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{1}}=\sqrt{9}=3 \\ {\sigma }_{2} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{2}}=\sqrt{1}=1\end{aligned}
$$

feedback.html:
Question 6
?

What are the singular values of the matrix A=[01−2−2−10]?

a
3 and 1
b
9 and 1
c
12 and 9
d
3 and 2
e
2 and 1
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The singular values of the matrix A are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix ATA.

First, we calculate ATA:

ATA=[01−2−2−10]T[01−2−2−10]=[0−2−11−20][01−2−2−10]=[5445]

Now, we solve the characteristic equation of ATA:

|ATA−λI|=0|5−λ445−λ|=0(5−λ)(5−λ)−16=0λ2−10λ+25−16=0λ2−10λ+9=0(λ−9)(λ−1)=0λ=9,1

Therefore, the singular values of A are as follows:

σ1=λ1=9=3σ2=λ2=1=1

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem: Given $h(x)=\frac{\sqrt{2x+7}}{\sqrt{x-7}},$ find $h(10).$
questions.worked_solution:
We replace $x$ with $10$ in the given expression, and simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}h(10) & =\frac{\sqrt{2x+7}}{\sqrt{x-7}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2(10)+7}}{\sqrt{10-7}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{27}}{\sqrt{3}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{27}{3}} \\  & =\sqrt{9} \\  & =3\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 2
questions.problem: Evaluate $\sqrt[3]{8a+1}$ at $a=10.$
questions.worked_solution:
We replace $a$ with $10$ in the given expression, and simplify as much as possible:

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt[3]{8a+1} & = \\ \sqrt[3]{8\cdot 10+1} & = \\ \sqrt[3]{80+1} & = \\ \sqrt[3]{81} & = \\ \sqrt[3]{27\cdot 3} & = \\ \sqrt[3]{{3}^{3}\cdot 3} & = \\ \sqrt[3]{{3}^{3}}\cdot \sqrt[3]{3} & = \\ 3\sqrt[3]{3} & \end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 3
questions.problem: Evaluate $\sqrt{x-3}$ for $x=15.$
questions.worked_solution:
We replace $x$ with $15$ in the given expression, and simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{x-3} & = \\ \sqrt{15-3} & = \\ \sqrt{12}\end{aligned}
$$

We can simplify even further using the product rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{12} & = \\ \sqrt{4\cdot 3} & = \\ \sqrt{{2}^{2}\cdot 3} & = \\ \sqrt{{2}^{2}}\cdot \sqrt{3} & = \\ 2\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Given $h(x)=\frac{\sqrt{2x+6}}{\sqrt{2x-1}},$ find $h(5).$
questions.worked_solution:

$$
\begin{aligned}h(5) & =\frac{\sqrt{2(5)+6}}{\sqrt{2(5)-1}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{10+6}}{\sqrt{10-1}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{16}}{\sqrt{9}} \\  & =\frac{4}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt[3]{7r+1} & = \\ \sqrt[3]{7(9)+1} & = \\ \sqrt[3]{63+1} & = \\ \sqrt[3]{64} & = \\ \sqrt[3]{{4}^{3}} & = \\ 4\end{aligned}

question.worked_solution:

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{x-3} & = \\ \sqrt{15-3} & = \\ \sqrt{12}\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{12} & = \\ \sqrt{4\cdot 3} & = \\ \sqrt{{2}^{2}\cdot 3} & = \\ \sqrt{{2}^{2}}\cdot \sqrt{3} & = \\ 2\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}
$$

question.problem: Given $h(x)=\frac{\sqrt{2x+6}}{\sqrt{2x-1}},$ find $h(5).$
question.worked_solution:
We replace $x$ with $5$ in the given expression, and simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}h(5) & =\frac{\sqrt{2(5)+6}}{\sqrt{2(5)-1}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{10+6}}{\sqrt{10-1}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{16}}{\sqrt{9}} \\  & =\frac{4}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 5
question.problem: Evaluate $\sqrt[3]{7r+1}$ at $r=9.$
question.worked_solution:
We replace $r$ with $9$ in the given expression, and simplify as much as possible:

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt[3]{7r+1} & = \\ \sqrt[3]{7(9)+1} & = \\ \sqrt[3]{63+1} & = \\ \sqrt[3]{64} & = \\ \sqrt[3]{{4}^{3}} & = \\ 4\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 1
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's rewrite the polynomial equation in the form ${P}_{n}(z)=0.$ To do this, we subtract all the terms from the right-hand side so that the right-hand side becomes $0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{z}^{3}-5{z}^{2} & =-2{z}^{3}+4{z}^{2}+30z \\ 3{z}^{3}-5{z}^{2} & =4{z}^{2}+30z \\ 3{z}^{3}-9{z}^{2} & =30z \\ 3{z}^{3}-9{z}^{2}-30z & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Next, notice that all of the terms of the polynomial have a common factor of $3z.$ We can factor out the $3z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}3{z}^{3}-9{z}^{2}-30z & =0 \\ 3z({z}^{2}-3z-10) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we factor the expression ${z}^{2}-3z-10$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}3z({z}^{2}-3z-10) & =0 \\ 3z(z-5)(z+2) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, by applying the zero product rule, the solutions are $z=0,$ $z=5,$ and $z=-2.$

questions.name: Question 2
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's rewrite the polynomial equation in the form ${P}_{n}(y)=0.$ To do this, we subtract all the terms from the right-hand side so that the right-hand side becomes $0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}6{y}^{3}+50{y}^{2}+100y & =5{y}^{2}+25y \\ 6{y}^{3}+45{y}^{2}+100y & =25y \\ 6{y}^{3}+45{y}^{2}+75y & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Next, notice that all of the terms of the polynomial have a common factor of $3y.$ We can factor out the $3y$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}6{y}^{3}+45{y}^{2}+75y & =0 \\ 3y(2{y}^{2}+15y+25) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we factor the expression $2{y}^{2}+15y+25$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}3y(2{y}^{2}+15y+25) & =0 \\ 3y(2y+5)(y+5) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, by applying the zero product rule, the solutions are $y=0,$ $y=-\frac{5}{2},$ and $y=-5.$

questions.name: Question 3
questions.problem: Determine the real roots of the cubic equation $2{x}^{3}-40{x}^{2}+35x=-3{x}^{3}.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's rewrite the polynomial equation in the form ${P}_{n}(x)=0.$ To do this, we subtract all the terms from the right-hand side so that the right-hand side becomes $0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}2{x}^{3}-40{x}^{2}+35x=-3{x}^{3} \\ 5{x}^{3}-40{x}^{2}+35x & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Next, notice that all of the terms of the polynomial have a common factor of $5x.$ We can factor out the $5x$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}5{x}^{3}-40{x}^{2}+35x & =0 \\ 5x({x}^{2}-8x+7) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we factor the expression ${x}^{2}-8x+7$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}5x({x}^{2}-8x+7) & =0 \\ 5x(x-1)(x-7) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, by applying the zero product rule, the solutions are $x=0,$ $x=1,$ and $x=7.$

questions.name: Question 4
questions.problem: Find the roots of the polynomial $p(y)=6{y}^{4}+3{y}^{3}-45{y}^{2}.$
questions.worked_solution:
To find the roots of the polynomial, we must solve the equation $p(y)=0,$ that is

$$
6{y}^{4}+3{y}^{3}-45{y}^{2}=0.
$$

First, notice that all of the terms of the polynomial have a common factor of $3{y}^{2}.$ We can factor out the $3{y}^{2}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}3{y}^{2}(2{y}^{2}+y-15) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we factor the expression $2{y}^{2}+y-15$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}3{y}^{2}(2{y}^{2}+y-15) & =0 \\ 3{y}^{2}(y+3)(2y-5) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, by applying the zero product rule, the solutions are $y=0,$ $y=-3,$ and $y=\frac{5}{2}.$

questions.name: Question 5
questions.problem: Find the roots of the polynomial $p(q)=24{q}^{5}-62{q}^{4}+14{q}^{3}.$
questions.worked_solution:
To find the roots of the polynomial, we must solve the equation $p(q)=0,$ that is

$$
24{q}^{5}-62{q}^{4}+14{q}^{3}=0.
$$

First, notice that all of the terms of the polynomial have a common factor of $2{q}^{3}.$ We can factor out the $2{q}^{3}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}2{q}^{3}(12{q}^{2}-31q+7) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we factor the expression $12{q}^{2}-31q+7$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}2{q}^{3}(12{q}^{2}-31q+7) & =0 \\ 2{q}^{3}(4q-1)(3q-7) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, by applying the zero product rule, the solutions are $q=0,$ $q=\frac{1}{4},$ and $q=\frac{7}{3}.$

questions.raw_html:
5.Solving a Higher-Order Polynomial Equation With No Constant Term?

Find the roots of the polynomial p(q)=24q5−62q4+14q3.

H
Tue, Oct 13th @ 10:50 AM|Elapsed: 0:14Correct

observed_steps.name: Question 1
observed_steps.worked_solution:
First, let's rewrite the polynomial equation in the form ${P}_{n}(z)=0.$ To do this, we subtract all the terms from the right-hand side so that the right-hand side becomes $0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{z}^{3}-5{z}^{2} & =-2{z}^{3}+4{z}^{2}+30z \\ 3{z}^{3}-5{z}^{2} & =4{z}^{2}+30z \\ 3{z}^{3}-9{z}^{2} & =30z \\ 3{z}^{3}-9{z}^{2}-30z & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Next, notice that all of the terms of the polynomial have a common factor of $3z.$ We can factor out the $3z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}3{z}^{3}-9{z}^{2}-30z & =0 \\ 3z({z}^{2}-3z-10) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we factor the expression ${z}^{2}-3z-10$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}3z({z}^{2}-3z-10) & =0 \\ 3z(z-5)(z+2) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, by applying the zero product rule, the solutions are $z=0,$ $z=5,$ and $z=-2.$

observed_steps.worked_solution:
First, let's rewrite the polynomial equation in the form ${P}_{n}(x)=0.$ To do this, we subtract all the terms from the right-hand side so that the right-hand side becomes $0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}2{x}^{3}-40{x}^{2}+35x=-3{x}^{3} \\ 5{x}^{3}-40{x}^{2}+35x & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Next, notice that all of the terms of the polynomial have a common factor of $5x.$ We can factor out the $5x$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}5{x}^{3}-40{x}^{2}+35x & =0 \\ 5x({x}^{2}-8x+7) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we factor the expression ${x}^{2}-8x+7$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}5x({x}^{2}-8x+7) & =0 \\ 5x(x-1)(x-7) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, by applying the zero product rule, the solutions are $x=0,$ $x=1,$ and $x=7.$

question.html:
Question 3
?

Determine the real roots of the cubic equation 2x3−40x2+35x=−3x3.

a
x=−1,0,1
b
x=−6,0,1
c
x=0,1,7
d
x=0,2,7
e
x=−1,0,8
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, let's rewrite the polynomial equation in the form Pn(x)=0. To do this, we subtract all the terms from the right-hand side so that the right-hand side becomes 0: 2x3−40x2+35x=−3x35x3−40x2+35x=0

Next, notice that all of the terms of the polynomial have a common factor of 5x. We can factor out the 5x as follows: 5x3−40x2+35x=05x(x2−8x+7)=0

Now, we factor the expression x2−8x+7 as follows: 5x(x2−8x+7)=05x(x−1)(x−7)=0

Finally, by applying the zero product rule, the solutions are x=0, x=1, and x=7.

6{y}^{4}+3{y}^{3}-45{y}^{2}=0.
$$

First, notice that all of the terms of the polynomial have a common factor of $3{y}^{2}.$ We can factor out the $3{y}^{2}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}3{y}^{2}(2{y}^{2}+y-15) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we factor the expression $2{y}^{2}+y-15$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}3{y}^{2}(2{y}^{2}+y-15) & =0 \\ 3{y}^{2}(y+3)(2y-5) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, by applying the zero product rule, the solutions are $y=0,$ $y=-3,$ and $y=\frac{5}{2}.$

Question 4

Find the roots of the polynomial p(y)=6y4+3y3−45y2.

a
y=0,32,5
b
y=−52,0,3
c
y=0,52,3
d
y=−3,0,52
e
y=−32,0,5
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

To find the roots of the polynomial, we must solve the equation p(y)=0, that is 6y4+3y3−45y2=0.

$$
24{q}^{5}-62{q}^{4}+14{q}^{3}=0.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}2{q}^{3}(12{q}^{2}-31q+7) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we factor the expression $12{q}^{2}-31q+7$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}2{q}^{3}(12{q}^{2}-31q+7) & =0 \\ 2{q}^{3}(4q-1)(3q-7) & =0\end{aligned}

Find the roots of the polynomial p(q)=24q5−62q4+14q3.

a
q=0,14,73
b
q=−23,0,12
c
q=−14,0,73
d
q=−73,0,12
e
q=0,12,23
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

To find the roots of the polynomial, we must solve the equation p(q)=0, that is 24q5−62q4+14q3=0.

First, notice that all of the terms of the polynomial have a common factor of 2q3. We can factor out the 2q3 as follows: 2q3(12q2−31q+7)=0

Now, we factor the expression 12q2−31q+7 as follows: 2q3(12q2−31q+7)=02q3(4q−1)(3q−7)=0

Finally, by applying the zero product rule, the solutions are q=0, q=14, and q=73.

question.name: Question 1
question.worked_solution:
First, let's rewrite the polynomial equation in the form ${P}_{n}(z)=0.$ To do this, we subtract all the terms from the right-hand side so that the right-hand side becomes $0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{z}^{3}-5{z}^{2} & =-2{z}^{3}+4{z}^{2}+30z \\ 3{z}^{3}-5{z}^{2} & =4{z}^{2}+30z \\ 3{z}^{3}-9{z}^{2} & =30z \\ 3{z}^{3}-9{z}^{2}-30z & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Next, notice that all of the terms of the polynomial have a common factor of $3z.$ We can factor out the $3z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}3{z}^{3}-9{z}^{2}-30z & =0 \\ 3z({z}^{2}-3z-10) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we factor the expression ${z}^{2}-3z-10$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}3z({z}^{2}-3z-10) & =0 \\ 3z(z-5)(z+2) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, by applying the zero product rule, the solutions are $z=0,$ $z=5,$ and $z=-2.$

question.html:
Question 1
?

If z3−5z2=−2z3+4z2+30z, then z=

a
z=−2,0,5
b
z=−3,0,5
c
z=−2,0,3
d
z=−3,0,2
e
z=−2,−3,5
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, let's rewrite the polynomial equation in the form Pn(z)=0. To do this, we subtract all the terms from the right-hand side so that the right-hand side becomes 0: z3−5z2=−2z3+4z2+30z3z3−5z2=4z2+30z3z3−9z2=30z3z3−9z2−30z=0

Next, notice that all of the terms of the polynomial have a common factor of 3z. We can factor out the 3z as follows: 3z3−9z2−30z=03z(z2−3z−10)=0

Now, we factor the expression z2−3z−10 as follows: 3z(z2−3z−10)=03z(z−5)(z+2)=0

Finally, by applying the zero product rule, the solutions are z=0, z=5, and z=−2.

\begin{aligned}{z}^{3}-5{z}^{2} & =-2{z}^{3}+4{z}^{2}+30z \\ 3{z}^{3}-5{z}^{2} & =4{z}^{2}+30z \\ 3{z}^{3}-9{z}^{2} & =30z \\ 3{z}^{3}-9{z}^{2}-30z & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Next, notice that all of the terms of the polynomial have a common factor of $3z.$ We can factor out the $3z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}3{z}^{3}-9{z}^{2}-30z & =0 \\ 3z({z}^{2}-3z-10) & =0\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}3z({z}^{2}-3z-10) & =0 \\ 3z(z-5)(z+2) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, by applying the zero product rule, the solutions are $z=0,$ $z=5,$ and $z=-2.$

Question 1
?

If z3−5z2=−2z3+4z2+30z, then z=

a
z=−2,0,5
b
z=−3,0,5
c
z=−2,0,3
d
z=−3,0,2
e
z=−2,−3,5
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, let's rewrite the polynomial equation in the form Pn(z)=0. To do this, we subtract all the terms from the right-hand side so that the right-hand side becomes 0: z3−5z2=−2z3+4z2+30z3z3−5z2=4z2+30z3z3−9z2=30z3z3−9z2−30z=0

Next, notice that all of the terms of the polynomial have a common factor of 3z. We can factor out the 3z as follows: 3z3−9z2−30z=03z(z2−3z−10)=0

Now, we factor the expression z2−3z−10 as follows: 3z(z2−3z−10)=03z(z−5)(z+2)=0

Finally, by applying the zero product rule, the solutions are z=0, z=5, and z=−2.

feedback.name: Question 1
feedback.worked_solution:
First, let's rewrite the polynomial equation in the form ${P}_{n}(z)=0.$ To do this, we subtract all the terms from the right-hand side so that the right-hand side becomes $0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{z}^{3}-5{z}^{2} & =-2{z}^{3}+4{z}^{2}+30z \\ 3{z}^{3}-5{z}^{2} & =4{z}^{2}+30z \\ 3{z}^{3}-9{z}^{2} & =30z \\ 3{z}^{3}-9{z}^{2}-30z & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Next, notice that all of the terms of the polynomial have a common factor of $3z.$ We can factor out the $3z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}3{z}^{3}-9{z}^{2}-30z & =0 \\ 3z({z}^{2}-3z-10) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we factor the expression ${z}^{2}-3z-10$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}3z({z}^{2}-3z-10) & =0 \\ 3z(z-5)(z+2) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, by applying the zero product rule, the solutions are $z=0,$ $z=5,$ and $z=-2.$

question.worked_solution:
First, let's rewrite the polynomial equation in the form ${P}_{n}(y)=0.$ To do this, we subtract all the terms from the right-hand side so that the right-hand side becomes $0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}6{y}^{3}+50{y}^{2}+100y & =5{y}^{2}+25y \\ 6{y}^{3}+45{y}^{2}+100y & =25y \\ 6{y}^{3}+45{y}^{2}+75y & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Next, notice that all of the terms of the polynomial have a common factor of $3y.$ We can factor out the $3y$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}6{y}^{3}+45{y}^{2}+75y & =0 \\ 3y(2{y}^{2}+15y+25) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we factor the expression $2{y}^{2}+15y+25$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}3y(2{y}^{2}+15y+25) & =0 \\ 3y(2y+5)(y+5) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, by applying the zero product rule, the solutions are $y=0,$ $y=-\frac{5}{2},$ and $y=-5.$

Question 2
?

If 6y3+50y2+100y=5y2+25y, then y=

a
y=0,52,5
b
y=−5,−52,0
c
y=−52,0,5
d
y=−52,0,52
e
y=−5,0,52
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, let's rewrite the polynomial equation in the form Pn(y)=0. To do this, we subtract all the terms from the right-hand side so that the right-hand side becomes 0: 6y3+50y2+100y=5y2+25y6y3+45y2+100y=25y6y3+45y2+75y=0

Next, notice that all of the terms of the polynomial have a common factor of 3y. We can factor out the 3y as follows: 6y3+45y2+75y=03y(2y2+15y+25)=0

Now, we factor the expression 2y2+15y+25 as follows: 3y(2y2+15y+25)=03y(2y+5)(y+5)=0

Finally, by applying the zero product rule, the solutions are y=0, y=−52, and y=−5.

last_observation.worked_solution:
First, let's rewrite the polynomial equation in the form ${P}_{n}(y)=0.$ To do this, we subtract all the terms from the right-hand side so that the right-hand side becomes $0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}6{y}^{3}+50{y}^{2}+100y & =5{y}^{2}+25y \\ 6{y}^{3}+45{y}^{2}+100y & =25y \\ 6{y}^{3}+45{y}^{2}+75y & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Next, notice that all of the terms of the polynomial have a common factor of $3y.$ We can factor out the $3y$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}6{y}^{3}+45{y}^{2}+75y & =0 \\ 3y(2{y}^{2}+15y+25) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we factor the expression $2{y}^{2}+15y+25$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}3y(2{y}^{2}+15y+25) & =0 \\ 3y(2y+5)(y+5) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, by applying the zero product rule, the solutions are $y=0,$ $y=-\frac{5}{2},$ and $y=-5.$

Question 2

If 6y3+50y2+100y=5y2+25y, then y=

a
y=0,52,5
b
y=−5,−52,0
c
y=−52,0,5
d
y=−52,0,52
e
y=−5,0,52
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, let's rewrite the polynomial equation in the form Pn(y)=0. To do this, we subtract all the terms from the right-hand side so that the right-hand side becomes 0: 6y3+50y2+100y=5y2+25y6y3+45y2+100y=25y6y3+45y2+75y=0

Next, notice that all of the terms of the polynomial have a common factor of 3y. We can factor out the 3y as follows: 6y3+45y2+75y=03y(2y2+15y+25)=0

Now, we factor the expression 2y2+15y+25 as follows: 3y(2y2+15y+25)=03y(2y+5)(y+5)=0

Finally, by applying the zero product rule, the solutions are y=0, y=−52, and y=−5.

question.name: Question 3
question.problem: Determine the real roots of the cubic equation $2{x}^{3}-40{x}^{2}+35x=-3{x}^{3}.$
question.worked_solution:
First, let's rewrite the polynomial equation in the form ${P}_{n}(x)=0.$ To do this, we subtract all the terms from the right-hand side so that the right-hand side becomes $0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}2{x}^{3}-40{x}^{2}+35x=-3{x}^{3} \\ 5{x}^{3}-40{x}^{2}+35x & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Next, notice that all of the terms of the polynomial have a common factor of $5x.$ We can factor out the $5x$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}5{x}^{3}-40{x}^{2}+35x & =0 \\ 5x({x}^{2}-8x+7) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we factor the expression ${x}^{2}-8x+7$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}5x({x}^{2}-8x+7) & =0 \\ 5x(x-1)(x-7) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, by applying the zero product rule, the solutions are $x=0,$ $x=1,$ and $x=7.$

Question 3
?

Determine the real roots of the cubic equation 2x3−40x2+35x=−3x3.

a
x=−1,0,1
b
x=−6,0,1
c
x=0,1,7
d
x=0,2,7
e
x=−1,0,8
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, let's rewrite the polynomial equation in the form Pn(x)=0. To do this, we subtract all the terms from the right-hand side so that the right-hand side becomes 0: 2x3−40x2+35x=−3x35x3−40x2+35x=0

Next, notice that all of the terms of the polynomial have a common factor of 5x. We can factor out the 5x as follows: 5x3−40x2+35x=05x(x2−8x+7)=0

Question 3
?

Determine the real roots of the cubic equation 2x3−40x2+35x=−3x3.

a
x=−1,0,1
b
x=−6,0,1
c
x=0,1,7
d
x=0,2,7
e
x=−1,0,8
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, let's rewrite the polynomial equation in the form Pn(x)=0. To do this, we subtract all the terms from the right-hand side so that the right-hand side becomes 0: 2x3−40x2+35x=−3x35x3−40x2+35x=0

Next, notice that all of the terms of the polynomial have a common factor of 5x. We can factor out the 5x as follows: 5x3−40x2+35x=05x(x2−8x+7)=0

Now, we factor the expression x2−8x+7 as follows: 5x(x2−8x+7)=05x(x−1)(x−7)=0

Finally, by applying the zero product rule, the solutions are x=0, x=1, and x=7.

Question 3
?

Determine the real roots of the cubic equation 2x3−40x2+35x=−3x3.

a
x=−1,0,1
b
x=−6,0,1
c
x=0,1,7
d
x=0,2,7
e
x=−1,0,8
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, let's rewrite the polynomial equation in the form Pn(x)=0. To do this, we subtract all the terms from the right-hand side so that the right-hand side becomes 0: 2x3−40x2+35x=−3x35x3−40x2+35x=0

Next, notice that all of the terms of the polynomial have a common factor of 5x. We can factor out the 5x as follows: 5x3−40x2+35x=05x(x2−8x+7)=0

Now, we factor the expression x2−8x+7 as follows: 5x(x2−8x+7)=05x(x−1)(x−7)=0

Finally, by applying the zero product rule, the solutions are x=0, x=1, and x=7.

question.name: Question 4
question.problem: Find the roots of the polynomial $p(y)=6{y}^{4}+3{y}^{3}-45{y}^{2}.$
question.worked_solution:
To find the roots of the polynomial, we must solve the equation $p(y)=0,$ that is

$$
6{y}^{4}+3{y}^{3}-45{y}^{2}=0.
$$

First, notice that all of the terms of the polynomial have a common factor of $3{y}^{2}.$ We can factor out the $3{y}^{2}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}3{y}^{2}(2{y}^{2}+y-15) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we factor the expression $2{y}^{2}+y-15$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}3{y}^{2}(2{y}^{2}+y-15) & =0 \\ 3{y}^{2}(y+3)(2y-5) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, by applying the zero product rule, the solutions are $y=0,$ $y=-3,$ and $y=\frac{5}{2}.$

Question 4
?

Find the roots of the polynomial p(y)=6y4+3y3−45y2.

a
y=0,32,5
b
y=−52,0,3
c
y=0,52,3
d
y=−3,0,52
e
y=−32,0,5
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

To find the roots of the polynomial, we must solve the equation p(y)=0, that is 6y4+3y3−45y2=0.

First, notice that all of the terms of the polynomial have a common factor of 3y2. We can factor out the 3y2 as follows: 3y2(2y2+y−15)=0

Now, we factor the expression 2y2+y−15 as follows: 3y2(2y2+y−15)=03y2(y+3)(2y−5)=0

Question 5
?

Find the roots of the polynomial p(q)=24q5−62q4+14q3.

a
q=0,14,73
b
q=−23,0,12
c
q=−14,0,73
d
q=−73,0,12
e
q=0,12,23
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

To find the roots of the polynomial, we must solve the equation p(q)=0, that is 24q5−62q4+14q3=0.

First, notice that all of the terms of the polynomial have a common factor of 2q3. We can factor out the 2q3 as follows: 2q3(12q2−31q+7)=0

Now, we factor the expression 12q2−31q+7 as follows: 2q3(12q2−31q+7)=02q3(4q−1)(3q−7)=0

Finally, by applying the zero product rule, the solutions are q=0, q=14, and q=73.

Find the roots of the polynomial p(q)=24q5−62q4+14q3.

a
q=0,14,73
b
q=−23,0,12
c
q=−14,0,73
d
q=−73,0,12
e
q=0,12,23
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

To find the roots of the polynomial, we must solve the equation p(q)=0, that is 24q5−62q4+14q3=0.

First, notice that all of the terms of the polynomial have a common factor of 2q3. We can factor out the 2q3 as follows: 2q3(12q2−31q+7)=0

Now, we factor the expression 12q2−31q+7 as follows: 2q3(12q2−31q+7)=02q3(4q−1)(3q−7)=0

Finally, by applying the zero product rule, the solutions are q=0, q=14, and q=73.

Question 5
?

Find the roots of the polynomial p(q)=24q5−62q4+14q3.

a
q=0,14,73
b
q=−23,0,12
c
q=−14,0,73
d
q=−73,0,12
e
q=0,12,23
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

To find the roots of the polynomial, we must solve the equation p(q)=0, that is 24q5−62q4+14q3=0.

First, notice that all of the terms of the polynomial have a common factor of 2q3. We can factor out the 2q3 as follows: 2q3(12q2−31q+7)=0

Now, we factor the expression 12q2−31q+7 as follows: 2q3(12q2−31q+7)=02q3(4q−1)(3q−7)=0

Finally, by applying the zero product rule, the solutions are q=0, q=14, and q=73.

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem:
Find ${\int }_{0}^{1}c\times f(t)\,\text{d}t$ 
given that 
${\int }_{0}^{1}f(t)\,\text{d}t=i+\frac{2}{3}\,j+k$ 
and 
$c=i+k.$
questions.worked_solution:
The cross-product rule states that

$$
{\int }_{0}^{1}c\times f(t)\,\text{d}t=c\times {\int }_{0}^{1}f(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

Applying the cross-product rule, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}c\times f(t)\,dt & =c\times {\int }_{0}^{1}f(t)\,dt \\  & =(i+k)\times (i+\frac{2}{3}\,j+k) \\  & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 1 & \frac{2}{3} & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ \frac{2}{3} & 1\end{aligned}|i-|\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}|j+|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 1 & \frac{2}{3}\end{aligned}|k \\  & =(0-\frac{2}{3})i-(1-1)j+(\frac{2}{3}-0)k \\  & =-\frac{2}{3}\,i+\frac{2}{3}\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Applying the Product Rules
questions.raw_html:
1.Applying the Product Rules?

Find ∫01c×f(t)dt given that ∫01f(t)dt=i+23j+k and c=i+k.

M
Tue, Oct 13th @ 10:49 AM|Elapsed: 0:17Correct

questions.name: Question 2
questions.worked_solution:
Let's reverse the limits of integration on the known result:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2}f(t)\,\text{d}t & =-{\int }_{2}^{0}f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =-⟨-4,\,-5,\,1⟩ \\  & =⟨4,\,5,\,-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, applying the vector addition rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2}f(t)+⟨2,\,1,\,3⟩\,\text{d}t & ={\int }_{0}^{2}f(t)\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{0}^{2}⟨2,\,1,\,3⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨4,\,5,\,-1⟩+{⟨2t,\,t,\,3t⟩|}_{0}^{2} \\  & =⟨4,\,5,\,-1⟩+⟨4,\,2,\,6⟩\text{ } \\  & =⟨8,\,7,\,5⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 3
questions.worked_solution:
Let's reverse the limits of integration on the known result:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{3}f(t)\,\text{d}t & =-{\int }_{3}^{0}f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =-⟨5,\,-1,\,-2⟩ \\  & =⟨-5,\,1,\,2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, applying the vector addition rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{3}f(t)+⟨-1,\,1,\,-1⟩\,\text{d}t & ={\int }_{0}^{3}f(t)\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{0}^{3}⟨-1,\,1,\,-1⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨-5,\,1,\,2⟩+{⟨-t,\,t,\,-t⟩|}_{0}^{3} \\  & =⟨-5,\,1,\,2⟩+⟨-3,\,3,\,-3⟩\text{ } \\  & =⟨-8,\,4,\,-1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 4
questions.problem:
Find ${\int }_{2}^{3}c\times f(t)\,\text{d}t$ 
given that 
${\int }_{2}^{3}f(t)\,\text{d}t=6\,i-4\,j+3\,k$ 
and 
$c=i-2\,j+2\,k.$
questions.worked_solution:
The cross-product rule states that

$$
{\int }_{2}^{3}c\times f(t)\,\text{d}t=c\times {\int }_{2}^{3}f(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

Applying the cross-product rule, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{2}^{3}c\times f(t)\,\text{d}t & =c\times {\int }_{2}^{3}f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =(i-2\,j+2\,k)\times (6\,i-4\,j+3\,k) \\  & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & -2 & 2 \\ 6 & -4 & 3\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 \\ -4 & 3\end{aligned}|i-|\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 6 & 3\end{aligned}|j+|\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ 6 & -4\end{aligned}|k \\  & =(-6+8)i-(3-12)j+(-4+12)k \\  & =2\,i+9\,j+8\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 5
questions.worked_solution:
Using the adjacent intervals rule, we have

$$
{\int }_{0}^{3}f(t)\,\text{d}t={\int }_{0}^{2}f(t)\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{2}^{3}f(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

We can rearrange the above as follows:

$$
{\int }_{2}^{3}f(t)\,\text{d}t={\int }_{0}^{3}f(t)\,\text{d}t-{\int }_{0}^{2}f(t)\,\text{d}t
$$

Finally, using the given information, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{2}^{3}f(t)\,\text{d}t & ={\int }_{0}^{3}f(t)\,\text{d}t-(-{\int }_{2}^{0}f(t)\,\text{d}t) \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}f(t)\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{2}^{0}f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨9,\,9,\,-6⟩+⟨-4,\,-6,\,4⟩ \\  & =⟨5,\,3,\,-2⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

observed_steps.name: Question 1
observed_steps.worked_solution:
The cross-product rule states that

$$
{\int }_{0}^{1}c\times f(t)\,\text{d}t=c\times {\int }_{0}^{1}f(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

Applying the cross-product rule, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}c\times f(t)\,dt & =c\times {\int }_{0}^{1}f(t)\,dt \\  & =(i+k)\times (i+\frac{2}{3}\,j+k) \\  & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 1 & \frac{2}{3} & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ \frac{2}{3} & 1\end{aligned}|i-|\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}|j+|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 1 & \frac{2}{3}\end{aligned}|k \\  & =(0-\frac{2}{3})i-(1-1)j+(\frac{2}{3}-0)k \\  & =-\frac{2}{3}\,i+\frac{2}{3}\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 1

$$

The cross-product rule states that

∫01c×f(t)dt=c×∫01f(t)dt.

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2}f(t)\,\text{d}t & =-{\int }_{2}^{0}f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =-⟨-4,\,-5,\,1⟩ \\  & =⟨4,\,5,\,-1⟩\end{aligned}

Therefore, applying the vector addition rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2}f(t)+⟨2,\,1,\,3⟩\,\text{d}t & ={\int }_{0}^{2}f(t)\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{0}^{2}⟨2,\,1,\,3⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨4,\,5,\,-1⟩+{⟨2t,\,t,\,3t⟩|}_{0}^{2} \\  & =⟨4,\,5,\,-1⟩+⟨4,\,2,\,6⟩\text{ } \\  & =⟨8,\,7,\,5⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the adjacent intervals rule, we have

$$
{\int }_{0}^{3}f(t)\,\text{d}t={\int }_{0}^{2}f(t)\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{2}^{3}f(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

We can rearrange the above as follows:

$$
{\int }_{2}^{3}f(t)\,\text{d}t={\int }_{0}^{3}f(t)\,\text{d}t-{\int }_{0}^{2}f(t)\,\text{d}t
$$

Finally, using the given information, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{2}^{3}f(t)\,\text{d}t & ={\int }_{0}^{3}f(t)\,\text{d}t-(-{\int }_{2}^{0}f(t)\,\text{d}t) \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}f(t)\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{2}^{0}f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨9,\,9,\,-6⟩+⟨-4,\,-6,\,4⟩ \\  & =⟨5,\,3,\,-2⟩.\end{aligned}

Question 5
?

Calculate ∫23f(t)dt given that ∫20f(t)dt=⟨−4,−6,4⟩ and ∫03f(t)dt=⟨9,9,−6⟩.

a
 ⟨5,3,4⟩
b
 ⟨13,−3,5⟩
c
 ⟨5,3,−2⟩
d
 ⟨5,−3,10⟩
e
 ⟨13,−3,10⟩
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Using the adjacent intervals rule, we have

∫03f(t)dt=∫02f(t)dt+∫23f(t)dt.

We can rearrange the above as follows:

∫23f(t)dt=∫03f(t)dt−∫02f(t)dt

Finally, using the given information, we get ∫23f(t)dt=∫03f(t)dt−(−∫20f(t)dt)=∫03f(t)dt+∫20f(t)dt=⟨9,9,−6⟩+⟨−4,−6,4⟩=⟨5,3,−2⟩.

question.name: Question 1
question.problem:
Find ${\int }_{0}^{1}c\times f(t)\,\text{d}t$ 
given that 
${\int }_{0}^{1}f(t)\,\text{d}t=i+\frac{2}{3}\,j+k$ 
and 
$c=i+k.$
question.worked_solution:
The cross-product rule states that

$$
{\int }_{0}^{1}c\times f(t)\,\text{d}t=c\times {\int }_{0}^{1}f(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

Applying the cross-product rule, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}c\times f(t)\,dt & =c\times {\int }_{0}^{1}f(t)\,dt \\  & =(i+k)\times (i+\frac{2}{3}\,j+k) \\  & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 1 & \frac{2}{3} & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ \frac{2}{3} & 1\end{aligned}|i-|\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}|j+|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 1 & \frac{2}{3}\end{aligned}|k \\  & =(0-\frac{2}{3})i-(1-1)j+(\frac{2}{3}-0)k \\  & =-\frac{2}{3}\,i+\frac{2}{3}\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

last_observation.name: Question 1
last_observation.worked_solution:
The cross-product rule states that

$$
{\int }_{0}^{1}c\times f(t)\,\text{d}t=c\times {\int }_{0}^{1}f(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

Applying the cross-product rule, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}c\times f(t)\,dt & =c\times {\int }_{0}^{1}f(t)\,dt \\  & =(i+k)\times (i+\frac{2}{3}\,j+k) \\  & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 1 & \frac{2}{3} & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ \frac{2}{3} & 1\end{aligned}|i-|\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}|j+|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 1 & \frac{2}{3}\end{aligned}|k \\  & =(0-\frac{2}{3})i-(1-1)j+(\frac{2}{3}-0)k \\  & =-\frac{2}{3}\,i+\frac{2}{3}\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

The cross-product rule states that

∫01c×f(t)dt=c×∫01f(t)dt.

Applying the cross-product rule, we have ∫01c×f(t)dt=c×∫01f(t)dt=(i+k)×(i+23j+k)=|ijk1011231|=|01231|i−|1111|j+|10123|k=(0−23)i−(1−1)j+(23−0)k=−23i+23k.

question.name: Question 2
question.worked_solution:
Let's reverse the limits of integration on the known result:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2}f(t)\,\text{d}t & =-{\int }_{2}^{0}f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =-⟨-4,\,-5,\,1⟩ \\  & =⟨4,\,5,\,-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, applying the vector addition rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2}f(t)+⟨2,\,1,\,3⟩\,\text{d}t & ={\int }_{0}^{2}f(t)\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{0}^{2}⟨2,\,1,\,3⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨4,\,5,\,-1⟩+{⟨2t,\,t,\,3t⟩|}_{0}^{2} \\  & =⟨4,\,5,\,-1⟩+⟨4,\,2,\,6⟩\text{ } \\  & =⟨8,\,7,\,5⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 2
?

Calculate ∫02f(t)+⟨2,1,3⟩dt given that ∫20f(t)dt=⟨−4,−5,1⟩.

a
⟨10,7,6⟩
b
⟨8,7,5⟩
c
⟨7,8,−5⟩
d
⟨0,−3,5⟩
e
⟨10,7,7⟩
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Let's reverse the limits of integration on the known result:

∫02f(t)dt=−∫20f(t)dt=−⟨−4,−5,1⟩=⟨4,5,−1⟩

Calculate ∫02f(t)+⟨2,1,3⟩dt given that ∫20f(t)dt=⟨−4,−5,1⟩.

a
⟨10,7,6⟩
b
⟨8,7,5⟩
c
⟨7,8,−5⟩
d
⟨0,−3,5⟩
e
⟨10,7,7⟩

Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Let's reverse the limits of integration on the known result:

∫02f(t)dt=−∫20f(t)dt=−⟨−4,−5,1⟩=⟨4,5,−1⟩

Therefore, applying the vector addition rule, we get

∫02f(t)+⟨2,1,3⟩dt=∫02f(t)dt+∫02⟨2,1,3⟩dt=⟨4,5,−1⟩+⟨2t,t,3t⟩|02=⟨4,5,−1⟩+⟨4,2,6⟩ =⟨8,7,5⟩.

a

b
⟨8,7,5⟩

⟨7,8,−5⟩

⟨0,−3,5⟩
e

EXPLANATION

Let's reverse the limits of integration on the known result:

∫02f(t)dt=−∫20f(t)dt=−⟨−4,−5,1⟩=⟨4,5,−1⟩

Therefore, applying the vector addition rule, we get

∫02f(t)+⟨2,1,3⟩dt=∫02f(t)dt+∫02⟨2,1,3⟩dt=⟨4,5,−1⟩+⟨2t,t,3t⟩|02=⟨4,5,−1⟩+⟨4,2,6⟩ =⟨8,7,5⟩.

question.worked_solution:
Let's reverse the limits of integration on the known result:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{3}f(t)\,\text{d}t & =-{\int }_{3}^{0}f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =-⟨5,\,-1,\,-2⟩ \\  & =⟨-5,\,1,\,2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, applying the vector addition rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{3}f(t)+⟨-1,\,1,\,-1⟩\,\text{d}t & ={\int }_{0}^{3}f(t)\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{0}^{3}⟨-1,\,1,\,-1⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨-5,\,1,\,2⟩+{⟨-t,\,t,\,-t⟩|}_{0}^{3} \\  & =⟨-5,\,1,\,2⟩+⟨-3,\,3,\,-3⟩\text{ } \\  & =⟨-8,\,4,\,-1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

last_observation.worked_solution:
Let's reverse the limits of integration on the known result:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{3}f(t)\,\text{d}t & =-{\int }_{3}^{0}f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =-⟨5,\,-1,\,-2⟩ \\  & =⟨-5,\,1,\,2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, applying the vector addition rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{3}f(t)+⟨-1,\,1,\,-1⟩\,\text{d}t & ={\int }_{0}^{3}f(t)\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{0}^{3}⟨-1,\,1,\,-1⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨-5,\,1,\,2⟩+{⟨-t,\,t,\,-t⟩|}_{0}^{3} \\  & =⟨-5,\,1,\,2⟩+⟨-3,\,3,\,-3⟩\text{ } \\  & =⟨-8,\,4,\,-1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 3
?

Calculate ∫03f(t)+⟨−1,1,−1⟩dt given that ∫30f(t)dt=⟨5,−1,−2⟩.

a
⟨2,−2,0⟩
b
⟨8,4,1⟩
c
⟨−8,2,1⟩
d
⟨−8,4,−1⟩
e
⟨2,2,−1⟩
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Let's reverse the limits of integration on the known result:

∫03f(t)dt=−∫30f(t)dt=−⟨5,−1,−2⟩=⟨−5,1,2⟩

Therefore, applying the vector addition rule, we get

∫03f(t)+⟨−1,1,−1⟩dt=∫03f(t)dt+∫03⟨−1,1,−1⟩dt=⟨−5,1,2⟩+⟨−t,t,−t⟩|03=⟨−5,1,2⟩+⟨−3,3,−3⟩ =⟨−8,4,−1⟩.

question.name: Question 4
question.problem:
Find ${\int }_{2}^{3}c\times f(t)\,\text{d}t$ 
given that 
${\int }_{2}^{3}f(t)\,\text{d}t=6\,i-4\,j+3\,k$ 
and 
$c=i-2\,j+2\,k.$
question.worked_solution:
The cross-product rule states that

$$
{\int }_{2}^{3}c\times f(t)\,\text{d}t=c\times {\int }_{2}^{3}f(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

Applying the cross-product rule, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{2}^{3}c\times f(t)\,\text{d}t & =c\times {\int }_{2}^{3}f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =(i-2\,j+2\,k)\times (6\,i-4\,j+3\,k) \\  & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & -2 & 2 \\ 6 & -4 & 3\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 \\ -4 & 3\end{aligned}|i-|\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 6 & 3\end{aligned}|j+|\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ 6 & -4\end{aligned}|k \\  & =(-6+8)i-(3-12)j+(-4+12)k \\  & =2\,i+9\,j+8\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 5
?

Calculate ∫23f(t)dt given that ∫20f(t)dt=⟨−4,−6,4⟩ and ∫03f(t)dt=⟨9,9,−6⟩.

a
 ⟨5,3,4⟩
b
 ⟨13,−3,5⟩
c
 ⟨5,3,−2⟩
d
 ⟨5,−3,10⟩
e
 ⟨13,−3,10⟩
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Using the adjacent intervals rule, we have

∫03f(t)dt=∫02f(t)dt+∫23f(t)dt.

We can rearrange the above as follows:

∫23f(t)dt=∫03f(t)dt−∫02f(t)dt

Finally, using the given information, we get ∫23f(t)dt=∫03f(t)dt−(−∫20f(t)dt)=∫03f(t)dt+∫20f(t)dt=⟨9,9,−6⟩+⟨−4,−6,4⟩=⟨5,3,−2⟩.

questions.name: Question 1
questions.worked_solution:
We will isolate a variable in one of the equations and then substitute it into the other equation. It so happens that the second equation is already solved for $u:$

$$
u=-v-2
$$

So, we replace $u$ with $-v-2$ in the first equation and solve for $v:$

$$
\begin{aligned}4u-6v & =-3 \\ 4(-v-2)-6v & =-3 \\ -4v-8-6v & =-3 \\ -10v & =5 \\ v & =-\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

If we now substitute $v=-\frac{1}{2}$ into $u=-v-2,$ then we can find the value of $u:$

$$
\begin{aligned}u & =-v-2 \\ u & =-(-\frac{1}{2})-2 \\ u & =-\frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the system of equations is $u=-\frac{3}{2},\,v=-\frac{1}{2},$ which can be expressed as $(-\frac{3}{2},-\frac{1}{2}).$

questions.name: Question 2
questions.worked_solution:
We will isolate a variable in one of the equations and then substitute it into the other equation. It doesn't matter which equation we pick first, so we choose the easiest one. In this case, the second equation looks like the easiest.

Using the second equation, we can isolate $x$ by adding $3y$ from both sides of the equation:

$$
x=3y-8
$$

So, we replace $x$ with $3y-8$ in the first equation and solve for $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}-2x+y & =-4 \\ -2(3y-8)+y & =-4 \\ -6y+16+y & =-4 \\ -5y & =-20 \\ y & =4\end{aligned}
$$

If we now substitute $y=4$ into $x=3y-8,$ then we can find the value of $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =3y-8 \\ x & =3(4)-8 \\ x & =12-8 \\ x & =4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the system of equations is $x=4,\,y=4,$ which can be expressed as $(4,4).$

questions.name: Question 3
questions.problem:
Given the system of equations below, what is the value of $y-x?$

$$
\{\begin{aligned}21x-9y=0 \\ 5y-15x+10=0\end{aligned}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
We number the equations so that we can refer to them more easily:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}21x-9y=0 & \,\,(1) \\ 5y-15x+10=0 & \,\,(2)\end{aligned}
$$

We will isolate a variable in one of the equations and then substitute it into the other equation. Using equation $(2),$ we can isolate $y$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}5y-15x+10 & =0 \\ 5y & =15x-10 \\ y & =3x-2\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we substitute $3x-2$  into equation $(1)$ and solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}21x-9y & =0 \\ 21x-9(3x-2) & =0 \\ 21x-27x+18 & =0 \\ -6x+18 & =0 \\ 18 & =6x \\ 3 & =x\end{aligned}
$$

If we now substitute $x=3$ into $y=3x-2,$ then we can find the value of $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =3x-2 \\ y & =3(3)-2 \\ y & =7\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the system of equations is $x=3,\,y=7.$ So,

$$
y-x=7-3=4.
$$
