questions.name: Question 4
questions.worked_solution:
We number the equations so that we can refer to them more easily:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}3p-6q=-18 & \,\,(1) \\ 4p+3q+2=0 & \,\,(2)\end{aligned}
$$

We will isolate a variable in one of the equations and then substitute it into the other equation. Using equation $(1),$ we can solve for $p$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}3p-6q & =-18 \\ 3p & =6q-18 \\ p & =2q-6\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we substitute $p=2q-6$ into equation $(2)$ and solve for $q:$

$$
\begin{aligned}4(2q-6)+3q+2 & =0 \\ 8q-24+3q+2 & =0 \\ 11q & =22 \\ q & =2\end{aligned}
$$

If we now substitute $q=2$ into equation $(1),$ then we can find the value of $p:$

$$
\begin{aligned}3p-6(2) & =-18 \\ 3p-12 & =-18 \\ 3p & =-6 \\ p & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the system of equations is $p=-2,\,q=2,$ which can be expressed as $(-2,2).$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Solving a System of Linear Equations Using Substitution
canonical_examples.problem:
Solve the following system of equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x-y=4 \\ x+2y=16\end{aligned}
$$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We will isolate a variable in one of the equations and then substitute it into the other equation. It doesn't matter which equation we pick first, so we choose the easiest one. In this case, the first equation looks like the easiest.

Using the first equation, we can isolate $x$ by adding $y$ to both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}x-y & =4 \\ x & =4+y\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we replace $x$ with $4+y$ in the second equation and solve for $y\mathbin{:}$

$$
\eqalign{
	x+2y &=16 \
	(4+y) + 2y &=16\
	4+3y &=16\
	3y &=12\
	y &=4
}
$$

If we now substitute $y=4$ into $x=4+y$, then we can find the value of $x\mathbin{:}$

$$
\eqalign{
	x &= 4 + y \
	   &= 4 + (4) \
	   &=8
}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the system of equations is $x = 8$ and $y = 4$, which can be written as $(8, 4).$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Solving a Challenging System of Linear Equations Using Substitution
canonical_examples.problem:
Solve the following system of equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}2u+9v-6=0 \\ 2u+6v-8=0\end{aligned}
$$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Sometimes, it's handy to assign a number to each equation in a system, so that we can refer to them more easily:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14180884/assets/77459b19bb1fd1f28e05e6f613e4e49af34595eae33eeeca584d65a289f7ea2c.svg)

We will isolate a variable in one of the equations and then substitute it into the other equation. Using equation $\color{blue}(2)$, we can solve for $u$ as follows:

$$
\eqalign{
	2u+6v-8 &= 0 \
2u+6v &= 8 \
2u &= 8 - 6v \
u &= \dfrac{8-6v}{2} \
u &= 4 - 3v
}
$$

Then, we substitute $u=4-3v$ into equation $\color{red}(1)$ and solve for $v\mathbin{:}$

$$
\eqalign{
	2u+9v-6 &= 0 \
	2(4-3v)+9v-6 &= 0 \
	8-6v+9v-6 &= 0 \
2+3v &= 0 \
3v &= -2 \
v &= -\dfrac{2}{3}
}
$$

If we now substitute $v=-\dfrac{2}{3}$ into equation $\color{red}(1)$, then we can find the value of $u\mathbin{:}$

$$
\eqalign{
	2u+9v-6 &= 0 \
	2u+9\left(-\dfrac{2}{3}\right) -6 &= 0 \
	2u-6-6 &= 0 \
	2u-12 &= 0 \
	2u &= 12 \
	u &= 6
}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the system of equations is $u=6$ and $v=-\dfrac{2}{3}$, which can be written as $\left(6,-\dfrac{2}{3}\right).$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Solving a Challenging System of Linear Equations Using Substitution

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
Suppose that we want to solve, *without* using graphs, the following system of linear equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x+y=4 \\ x-2=y\,\end{aligned}
$$

In order to solve the system without a graph, we will need to combine the equations into a single equation that can be solved using algebraic manipulation.

One way to combine the equations is called the **substitution method.** To use the substitution method, we substitute for one variable in terms of the other.

For instance, notice that we can make $y$ the subject of the second equation:

$$
\color{red}y=x - 2
$$

Substituting this expression for $y$ into the first equation, we get an equation that we can solve for $x\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}x+y & =4 \\ x+(x-2) & =4 \\ 2x-2 & =4 \\ 2x & =6 \\ x & =3\end{aligned}
$$

So, the solution must have $x=3.$ But we also need to figure out what $y$ is. We can do this by substituting $x=3$ back into the second equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =x-2 \\ y & =3-2 \\ y & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the system of equations is $x = 3$ and $y = 1$, which can be written as $\left(3, 1\right).$

**Note:** Whenever we isolate the variable in one equation, we have to substitute it into the *other* equation. We cannot substitute a variable into the same equation it came from, because this will not give us any more information about the variable.

observed_steps.worked_solution:
We will isolate a variable in one of the equations and then substitute it into the other equation. It doesn't matter which equation we pick first, so we choose the easiest one. In this case, the first equation looks like the easiest.

Using the first equation, we can isolate $x$ by adding $y$ to both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}x-y & =4 \\ x & =4+y\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we replace $x$ with $4+y$ in the second equation and solve for $y\mathbin{:}$

$$
\eqalign{
	x+2y &=16 \
	(4+y) + 2y &=16\
	4+3y &=16\
	3y &=12\
	y &=4
}
$$

If we now substitute $y=4$ into $x=4+y$, then we can find the value of $x\mathbin{:}$

$$
\eqalign{
	x &= 4 + y \
	   &= 4 + (4) \
	   &=8
}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the system of equations is $x = 8$ and $y = 4$, which can be written as $(8, 4).$

observed_steps.worked_solution:
We will isolate a variable in one of the equations and then substitute it into the other equation. It so happens that the second equation is already solved for $u:$

$$
u=-v-2
$$

So, we replace $u$ with $-v-2$ in the first equation and solve for $v:$

$$
\begin{aligned}4u-6v & =-3 \\ 4(-v-2)-6v & =-3 \\ -4v-8-6v & =-3 \\ -10v & =5 \\ v & =-\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

If we now substitute $v=-\frac{1}{2}$ into $u=-v-2,$ then we can find the value of $u:$

$$
\begin{aligned}u & =-v-2 \\ u & =-(-\frac{1}{2})-2 \\ u & =-\frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the system of equations is $u=-\frac{3}{2},\,v=-\frac{1}{2},$ which can be expressed as $(-\frac{3}{2},-\frac{1}{2}).$

observed_steps.worked_solution:
We will isolate a variable in one of the equations and then substitute it into the other equation. It doesn't matter which equation we pick first, so we choose the easiest one. In this case, the second equation looks like the easiest.

Using the second equation, we can isolate $x$ by adding $3y$ from both sides of the equation:

$$
x=3y-8
$$

So, we replace $x$ with $3y-8$ in the first equation and solve for $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}-2x+y & =-4 \\ -2(3y-8)+y & =-4 \\ -6y+16+y & =-4 \\ -5y & =-20 \\ y & =4\end{aligned}
$$

If we now substitute $y=4$ into $x=3y-8,$ then we can find the value of $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =3y-8 \\ x & =3(4)-8 \\ x & =12-8 \\ x & =4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the system of equations is $x=4,\,y=4,$ which can be expressed as $(4,4).$

observed_steps.worked_solution:
Sometimes, it's handy to assign a number to each equation in a system, so that we can refer to them more easily:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14180884/assets/84febd8a66a64c81558ce4235552e9b9a103d9418fa44d4f94ab7d91fbcc605a.svg)

We will isolate a variable in one of the equations and then substitute it into the other equation. Using equation $\color{blue}(2)$, we can solve for $u$ as follows:

$$
\eqalign{
	2u+6v-8 &= 0 \
2u+6v &= 8 \
2u &= 8 - 6v \
u &= \dfrac{8-6v}{2} \
u &= 4 - 3v
}
$$

Then, we substitute $u=4-3v$ into equation $\color{red}(1)$ and solve for $v\mathbin{:}$

$$
\eqalign{
	2u+9v-6 &= 0 \
	2(4-3v)+9v-6 &= 0 \
	8-6v+9v-6 &= 0 \
2+3v &= 0 \
3v &= -2 \
v &= -\dfrac{2}{3}
}
$$

If we now substitute $v=-\dfrac{2}{3}$ into equation $\color{red}(1)$, then we can find the value of $u\mathbin{:}$

$$
\eqalign{
	2u+9v-6 &= 0 \
	2u+9\left(-\dfrac{2}{3}\right) -6 &= 0 \
	2u-6-6 &= 0 \
	2u-12 &= 0 \
	2u &= 12 \
	u &= 6
}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the system of equations is $u=6$ and $v=-\dfrac{2}{3}$, which can be written as $\left(6,-\dfrac{2}{3}\right).$

observed_steps.name: Question 3
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Solving a Challenging System of Linear Equations Using Substitution
observed_steps.worked_solution:
We number the equations so that we can refer to them more easily:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}21x-9y=0 & \,\,(1) \\ 5y-15x+10=0 & \,\,(2)\end{aligned}
$$

We will isolate a variable in one of the equations and then substitute it into the other equation. Using equation $(2),$ we can isolate $y$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}5y-15x+10 & =0 \\ 5y & =15x-10 \\ y & =3x-2\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we substitute $3x-2$  into equation $(1)$ and solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}21x-9y & =0 \\ 21x-9(3x-2) & =0 \\ 21x-27x+18 & =0 \\ -6x+18 & =0 \\ 18 & =6x \\ 3 & =x\end{aligned}
$$

If we now substitute $x=3$ into $y=3x-2,$ then we can find the value of $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =3x-2 \\ y & =3(3)-2 \\ y & =7\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the system of equations is $x=3,\,y=7.$ So,

$$
y-x=7-3=4.
$$

We number the equations so that we can refer to them more easily:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}3p-6q=-18 & \,\,(1) \\ 4p+3q+2=0 & \,\,(2)\end{aligned}
$$

We will isolate a variable in one of the equations and then substitute it into the other equation. Using equation $(1),$ we can solve for $p$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}3p-6q & =-18 \\ 3p & =6q-18 \\ p & =2q-6\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we substitute $p=2q-6$ into equation $(2)$ and solve for $q:$

$$
\begin{aligned}4(2q-6)+3q+2 & =0 \\ 8q-24+3q+2 & =0 \\ 11q & =22 \\ q & =2\end{aligned}
$$

If we now substitute $q=2$ into equation $(1),$ then we can find the value of $p:$

$$
\begin{aligned}3p-6(2) & =-18 \\ 3p-12 & =-18 \\ 3p & =-6 \\ p & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the system of equations is $p=-2,\,q=2,$ which can be expressed as $(-2,2).$

question.name: Question 2
question.worked_solution:
We will isolate a variable in one of the equations and then substitute it into the other equation. It doesn't matter which equation we pick first, so we choose the easiest one. In this case, the second equation looks like the easiest.

Using the second equation, we can isolate $x$ by adding $3y$ from both sides of the equation:

$$
x=3y-8
$$

So, we replace $x$ with $3y-8$ in the first equation and solve for $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}-2x+y & =-4 \\ -2(3y-8)+y & =-4 \\ -6y+16+y & =-4 \\ -5y & =-20 \\ y & =4\end{aligned}
$$

If we now substitute $y=4$ into $x=3y-8,$ then we can find the value of $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =3y-8 \\ x & =3(4)-8 \\ x & =12-8 \\ x & =4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the system of equations is $x=4,\,y=4,$ which can be expressed as $(4,4).$

question.name: Question 3
question.problem:
Given the system of equations below, what is the value of $y-x?$

$$
\{\begin{aligned}21x-9y=0 \\ 5y-15x+10=0\end{aligned}
$$
question.worked_solution:
We number the equations so that we can refer to them more easily:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}21x-9y=0 & \,\,(1) \\ 5y-15x+10=0 & \,\,(2)\end{aligned}
$$

We will isolate a variable in one of the equations and then substitute it into the other equation. Using equation $(2),$ we can isolate $y$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}5y-15x+10 & =0 \\ 5y & =15x-10 \\ y & =3x-2\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we substitute $3x-2$  into equation $(1)$ and solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}21x-9y & =0 \\ 21x-9(3x-2) & =0 \\ 21x-27x+18 & =0 \\ -6x+18 & =0 \\ 18 & =6x \\ 3 & =x\end{aligned}
$$

If we now substitute $x=3$ into $y=3x-2,$ then we can find the value of $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =3x-2 \\ y & =3(3)-2 \\ y & =7\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the system of equations is $x=3,\,y=7.$ So,

$$
y-x=7-3=4.
$$

Given the system of equations below, what is the value of y−x?

{21x−9y=05y−15x+10=0

4

Correct
EXPLANATION

We number the equations so that we can refer to them more easily:

{21x−9y=0(1)5y−15x+10=0(2)

We will isolate a variable in one of the equations and then substitute it into the other equation. Using equation (2), we can isolate y as follows:

5y−15x+10=05y=15x−10y=3x−2

Then, we substitute 3x−2 into equation (1) and solve for x:

21x−9y=021x−9(3x−2)=021x−27x+18=0−6x+18=018=6x3=x

If we now substitute x=3 into y=3x−2, then we can find the value of y: y=3x−2y=3(3)−2y=7

Therefore, the solution to the system of equations is x=3,y=7. So, y−x=7−3=4.

solution.reasoning: The first equation gives y=7x/3. The second gives y=3x-2. Substitution yields 7x/3=3x-2, so 7x=9x-6 and x=3. Then y=7, hence y-x=4, choice c. No Math Academy answer or grade for this question is captured; the worked example concerns a different system.

feedback.problem:
Given the system of equations below, what is the value of $y-x?$

$$
\{\begin{aligned}21x-9y=0 \\ 5y-15x+10=0\end{aligned}
$$
feedback.worked_solution:
We number the equations so that we can refer to them more easily:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}21x-9y=0 & \,\,(1) \\ 5y-15x+10=0 & \,\,(2)\end{aligned}
$$

We will isolate a variable in one of the equations and then substitute it into the other equation. Using equation $(2),$ we can isolate $y$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}5y-15x+10 & =0 \\ 5y & =15x-10 \\ y & =3x-2\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we substitute $3x-2$  into equation $(1)$ and solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}21x-9y & =0 \\ 21x-9(3x-2) & =0 \\ 21x-27x+18 & =0 \\ -6x+18 & =0 \\ 18 & =6x \\ 3 & =x\end{aligned}
$$

If we now substitute $x=3$ into $y=3x-2,$ then we can find the value of $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =3x-2 \\ y & =3(3)-2 \\ y & =7\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the system of equations is $x=3,\,y=7.$ So,

$$
y-x=7-3=4.
$$

question.name: Question 4
question.worked_solution:
We number the equations so that we can refer to them more easily:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}3p-6q=-18 & \,\,(1) \\ 4p+3q+2=0 & \,\,(2)\end{aligned}
$$

We will isolate a variable in one of the equations and then substitute it into the other equation. Using equation $(1),$ we can solve for $p$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}3p-6q & =-18 \\ 3p & =6q-18 \\ p & =2q-6\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we substitute $p=2q-6$ into equation $(2)$ and solve for $q:$

$$
\begin{aligned}4(2q-6)+3q+2 & =0 \\ 8q-24+3q+2 & =0 \\ 11q & =22 \\ q & =2\end{aligned}
$$

If we now substitute $q=2$ into equation $(1),$ then we can find the value of $p:$

$$
\begin{aligned}3p-6(2) & =-18 \\ 3p-12 & =-18 \\ 3p & =-6 \\ p & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the system of equations is $p=-2,\,q=2,$ which can be expressed as $(-2,2).$

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem:
Consider the vector space ${R}_{2}[t]$ of all polynomials in the variable $t$ of degree at most $2,$ and its subset $A$ containing all polynomials of the form $a{t}^{2},$ where $a\in R.$

Which of the following statements are true?

I. $A$ is closed under polynomial addition

II. $A$ is closed under scalar multiplication

III. $A$ is a subspace of ${R}_{2}[t]$

IV. $A$ is **not** a subspace of ${R}_{2}[t]$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that a subset of a vector space is a subspace if it's closed under addition and scalar multiplication.

With that in mind, let's examine each statement in turn.

- Statement I is true. If $f(t)={a}_{1}{t}^{2}$ and $g(t)={a}_{2}{t}^{2}$ are two polynomials from $A,$ then

$$
\begin{aligned}f(t)+g(t) & ={a}_{1}{t}^{2}+{a}_{2}{t}^{2} \\  & =({a}_{1}+{a}_{2}){t}^{2},\end{aligned}
$$

which is a polynomial from $A.$ So, $A$ is closed under addition.

- Statement II is true. If $f(t)=a{t}^{2}\in A$ and $k\in R,$ then 

$$
\begin{aligned}kf(t) & =k(a{t}^{2}) \\  & =(ka){t}^{2},\end{aligned}
$$

which is a polynomial from $A.$ So, $A$ is closed under scalar multiplication.

- Statement III is true while statement IV is false. $A$ is a subspace because it's closed under addition and scalar multiplication.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III only."

questions.name: Question 2
questions.problem:
Consider the vector space ${\text{M}}_{2}(R)$ of all $2\times 2$ matrices over $R$ and its subset $A=\{[\begin{aligned}0 & a \\ b & 0\end{aligned}]\,|\,a,b\in R\}.$  

Which of the following statements are true?

I. $A$ is closed under matrix addition

II. $A$ is closed under scalar multiplication

III. $A$ is a subspace of ${\text{M}}_{2}(R)$

IV. $A$ is **not** a subspace of ${\text{M}}_{2}(R)$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that a subset of a vector space is a subspace if it's closed under addition and scalar multiplication.

With that in mind, let's examine each statement in turn.

- Statement I is true. If ${A}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}0 & {a}_{1} \\ {b}_{1} & 0\end{aligned}]$ and ${A}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}0 & {a}_{2} \\ {b}_{2} & 0\end{aligned}]$ are two matrices from $A,$ then 

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{1}+{A}_{2} & =[\begin{aligned}0 & {a}_{1} \\ {b}_{1} & 0\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}0 & {a}_{2} \\ {b}_{2} & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & {a}_{1}+{a}_{2} \\ {b}_{1}+{b}_{2} & 0\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

 
which is a matrix from $A.$ So, $A$ is closed under addition.

- Statement II is true. If $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & a \\ b & 0\end{aligned}]$ is an element of $A$ and $k\in R,$ then 

$$
\begin{aligned}kA & =k[\begin{aligned}0 & a \\ b & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & ka \\ kb & 0\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

which is a matrix from $A.$ So, $A$ is closed under scalar multiplication.

- Statement III is true, while statement IV is false. $A$ is a subspace because it's closed under addition and scalar multiplication.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III only."

questions.worked_solution:
Recall that a subset of a vector space is a subspace if it's closed under addition and scalar multiplication.

With that in mind, let's examine each statement in turn. 

- Statement I is false. For example, if ${A}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]$ and ${A}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}],$ then
${A}_{1}$ and ${A}_{2}$ each contain a row consisting only of zeros, so they are not invertible. However,

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{1}+{A}_{2} & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

is invertible. So, $S$ is *not* closed under addition.

- Statement II is true. Indeed, if $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix that is not invertible then $det(A)=0$ and therefore for all $\alpha \in R$ 

$$
det(\alpha A)={\alpha }^{2}\cdot det(A)={\alpha }^{2}\cdot 0=0.
$$

Therefore,  $S$ is closed under scalar multiplication.

- Statement III is false, while statement IV is true. $S$ is a *not* subspace because it's not closed under addition.

  1. A is closed under polynomial addition
  2. A is closed under scalar multiplication
  3. A is a subspace of R2[t]
  4. A is not a subspace of R2[t]
a
IV only
b
II only
c
I and IV only
d
II and IV only
e
I, II, and III only
Submit
Correct

Recall that a subset of a vector space is a subspace if it's closed under addition and scalar multiplication.

Consider the vector space ${\text{M}}_{2}(R)$ of all $2\times 2$ matrices over $R$ and its subset $A=\{[\begin{aligned}0 & a \\ b & 0\end{aligned}]\,|\,a,b\in R\}.$  

Which of the following statements are true?

I. $A$ is closed under matrix addition

II. $A$ is closed under scalar multiplication

III. $A$ is a subspace of ${\text{M}}_{2}(R)$

IV. $A$ is **not** a subspace of ${\text{M}}_{2}(R)$
question.worked_solution:
Recall that a subset of a vector space is a subspace if it's closed under addition and scalar multiplication.

With that in mind, let's examine each statement in turn.

- Statement I is true. If ${A}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}0 & {a}_{1} \\ {b}_{1} & 0\end{aligned}]$ and ${A}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}0 & {a}_{2} \\ {b}_{2} & 0\end{aligned}]$ are two matrices from $A,$ then 

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{1}+{A}_{2} & =[\begin{aligned}0 & {a}_{1} \\ {b}_{1} & 0\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}0 & {a}_{2} \\ {b}_{2} & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & {a}_{1}+{a}_{2} \\ {b}_{1}+{b}_{2} & 0\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

 
which is a matrix from $A.$ So, $A$ is closed under addition.

- Statement II is true. If $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & a \\ b & 0\end{aligned}]$ is an element of $A$ and $k\in R,$ then 

$$
\begin{aligned}kA & =k[\begin{aligned}0 & a \\ b & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & ka \\ kb & 0\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

which is a matrix from $A.$ So, $A$ is closed under scalar multiplication.

- Statement III is true, while statement IV is false. $A$ is a subspace because it's closed under addition and scalar multiplication.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III only."

question.name: Question 3
question.problem:
Consider the vector space ${\text{M}}_{2}(R)$ of all $2\times 2$ matrices over $R,$ and its subset $S$ containing $2\times 2$ matrices that are not invertible. 

Which of the following statements are true?

I. $S$ is closed under matrix addition

II. $S$ is closed under scalar multiplication

III. $S$ is a subspace of ${\text{M}}_{2}(R)$

IV. $S$ is **not** a subspace of ${\text{M}}_{2}(R)$
question.worked_solution:
Recall that a subset of a vector space is a subspace if it's closed under addition and scalar multiplication.

With that in mind, let's examine each statement in turn. 

- Statement I is false. For example, if ${A}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]$ and ${A}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}],$ then
${A}_{1}$ and ${A}_{2}$ each contain a row consisting only of zeros, so they are not invertible. However,

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{1}+{A}_{2} & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

is invertible. So, $S$ is *not* closed under addition.

- Statement II is true. Indeed, if $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix that is not invertible then $det(A)=0$ and therefore for all $\alpha \in R$ 

$$
det(\alpha A)={\alpha }^{2}\cdot det(A)={\alpha }^{2}\cdot 0=0.
$$

Therefore,  $S$ is closed under scalar multiplication.

- Statement III is false, while statement IV is true. $S$ is a *not* subspace because it's not closed under addition.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and IV only."

Consider the region $R$ shown above. Let the function $f(x,y)$ be defined as

$$
f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}{e}^{x}, & (x,y)\in S, \\ {x}^{2}+y, & (x,y)\in T, \\ 0, & (x,y)\in U.\end{aligned}
$$

Then,

$$
{∬}_{R}f(x,y)\text{ }\text{d}A=
$$
questions.worked_solution:
First, notice that the domain $R$ can be represented as a union of three sub-domains, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}R & =S\cup T\cup U.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we can write

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{S}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{T}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{U}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{S}{e}^{x}\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{T}({x}^{2}+y)\text{d}A+{∬}_{U}0\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{S}{e}^{x}\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{T}({x}^{2}+y)\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 3
questions.problem: Calculate ${∬}_{R}({x}^{2}-y+1)\,\text{d}A$,  where $R=[-3,0]\times [0,4].$
questions.worked_solution:
Using the linearity property of double integrals, we can write

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}({x}^{2}-y+1)\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{R}{x}^{2}\text{ }\text{d}A-{∬}_{R}y\text{ }\text{d}A+{∬}_{R}\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

The function under the first integral is independent of $y.$ So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}{x}^{2}\text{ }\text{d}A & =(4-0){\int }_{-3}^{0}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =4[\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}]_{-3}^{0} \\  & =4(\frac{{0}^{3}}{3}-\frac{(-3)^{3}}{3}) \\  & =36.\end{aligned}
$$

The function under the second integral is independent of $x.$ So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}y\text{ }\text{d}A & =(0-(-3)){\int }_{0}^{4}y\,\text{d}y \\  & =3[\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}]_{0}^{4} \\  & =3(\frac{{4}^{2}}{2}-\frac{{0}^{2}}{2}) \\  & =24.\end{aligned}
$$

The third integral is the double integral of unity:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}\text{d}A=\text{Area}(R)=3\cdot 4=12\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, combining our results, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}({x}^{2}-y+1)\,\text{d}A=36-24+12=24.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 4
questions.problem:
Evaluate the double integral ${∬}_{R}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A$, where

$$
f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡y,\, & \text{if}\,-1<x<1,\,0<y<\pi , \\ x\operatorname{sin}⁡y,\, & \text{if}\,1<x<2,\,0<y<\pi ,\end{aligned}
$$

and  $R$ is the domain of $f.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, notice that we have $R={R}_{1}\cup {R}_{2}$, where ${R}_{1}=(-1,1)\times (0,\pi )$ and ${R}_{2}=(1,2)\times (0,\pi ).$ So, we can write

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A= & ={∬}_{{R}_{1}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{{R}_{2}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{{R}_{1}}\operatorname{cos}⁡y\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{{R}_{2}}x\operatorname{sin}⁡y\,\text{d}A \\  & =(1-(-1)){\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡y\,\text{d}y+({\int }_{1}^{2}x\,\text{d}x)({\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡y\,\text{d}y) \\  & =2[\operatorname{sin}⁡y]_{0}^{\pi }+[\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}]_{1}^{2}\cdot [-\operatorname{cos}⁡y]_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =2(0)+(2-\frac{1}{2})\cdot (-(-1)+1) \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 5
questions.problem:
Given that $C$ and $D$ are finite, non-overlapping regions and that

$$
{∬}_{C}f(x,y)\text{ }\text{d}A=2,\,{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }\text{d}A=7,
$$

find the value of 

$$
{∬}_{C\cup D}\frac{1}{3}f(x,y)\text{ }\text{d}A.
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Using the linearity and additivity of double integrals, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{C\cup D}5f(x,y)\text{ }\text{d}A & =\frac{1}{3}{∬}_{C\cup D}f(x,y)\text{ }\text{d}A \\  & =\frac{1}{3}({∬}_{C}f(x,y)\text{ }\text{d}A+{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }\text{d}A) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(7+2) \\  & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Given that C and D are finite, non-overlapping regions and that ∬Cf(x,y) dA=2,∬Df(x,y) dA=7, find the value of ∬C∪D13f(x,y) dA.

$$

Question 1
?

Consider the region R shown above. Let the function f(x,y) be defined as f(x,y)={ex,(x,y)∈S,x2+y,(x,y)∈T,0,(x,y)∈U. Then, ∬Rf(x,y) dA=

a
∬SexdA+∬TxdA+∬U(x2+y)dA
b
∬SexdA+∬T(x2+y)dA+∬UxdA
c
∬S(x2+y)dA+∬TexdA+∬UdA
d
∬SexdA+∬T(x2+y)dA
e
∬SyexdA+∬Tx2dA+∬UdA
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, notice that the domain R can be represented as a union of three sub-domains, as follows:

R=S∪T∪U.

So, we can write

∬Rf(x,y)dA=∬Sf(x,y)dA+∬Tf(x,y)dA+∬Uf(x,y)dA=∬SexdA+∬T(x2+y)dA+∬U0dA=∬SexdA+∬T(x2+y)dA.

Question 2
?

Evaluate the double integral ∬Rf(x,y)dA, where f(x,y)={3x2,if0<x<1,0<y<1,2x ey,if0<x<1,1<y<2, and R is the domain of f.

a
 1−e2
b
 1+e2+e
c
 1+e2−e
d
 1−e2
e
 1+e2
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, notice that we have R=R1∪R2, where R1=(0,1)×(0,1) and R2=(0,1)×(1,2). So, we can write

∬Rf(x,y)dA=∬R1f(x,y)dA+∬R2f(x,y)dA=∬R13x2dA+∬R22x eydA=(1−0)∫013x2dy+(∫012xdx)(∫12eydy)=x3|01+(x2|01)⋅(ey|12)=1+1⋅(e2−e1)=1+e2−e.

observed_steps.name: Question 3
observed_steps.worked_solution:
Using the linearity property of double integrals, we can write

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}({x}^{2}-y+1)\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{R}{x}^{2}\text{ }\text{d}A-{∬}_{R}y\text{ }\text{d}A+{∬}_{R}\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

The function under the first integral is independent of $y.$ So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}{x}^{2}\text{ }\text{d}A & =(4-0){\int }_{-3}^{0}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =4[\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}]_{-3}^{0} \\  & =4(\frac{{0}^{3}}{3}-\frac{(-3)^{3}}{3}) \\  & =36.\end{aligned}
$$

The function under the second integral is independent of $x.$ So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}y\text{ }\text{d}A & =(0-(-3)){\int }_{0}^{4}y\,\text{d}y \\  & =3[\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}]_{0}^{4} \\  & =3(\frac{{4}^{2}}{2}-\frac{{0}^{2}}{2}) \\  & =24.\end{aligned}
$$

The third integral is the double integral of unity:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}\text{d}A=\text{Area}(R)=3\cdot 4=12\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, combining our results, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}({x}^{2}-y+1)\,\text{d}A=36-24+12=24.\end{aligned}
$$

The function under the first integral is independent of $y.$ So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}{x}^{2}\text{ }\text{d}A & =(4-0){\int }_{-3}^{0}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =4[\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}]_{-3}^{0} \\  & =4(\frac{{0}^{3}}{3}-\frac{(-3)^{3}}{3}) \\  & =36.\end{aligned}
$$

The function under the second integral is independent of $x.$ So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}y\text{ }\text{d}A & =(0-(-3)){\int }_{0}^{4}y\,\text{d}y \\  & =3[\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}]_{0}^{4} \\  & =3(\frac{{4}^{2}}{2}-\frac{{0}^{2}}{2}) \\  & =24.\end{aligned}

question.html:
Question 3
?

Calculate ∬R(x2−y+1)dA, where R=[−3,0]×[0,4].

a
0
b
12
c
24
d
36
e
72
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Using the linearity property of double integrals, we can write

∬R(x2−y+1)dA=∬Rx2 dA−∬Ry dA+∬RdA.

The function under the first integral is independent of y. So, we have

∬Rx2 dA=(4−0)∫−30x2dx=4[x33]−30=4(033−(−3)33)=36.

The function under the second integral is independent of x. So, we have

∬Ry dA=(0−(−3))∫04ydy=3[y22]04=3(422−022)=24.

The third integral is the double integral of unity:

∬RdA=Area(R)=3⋅4=12

Finally, combining our results, we obtain

∬R(x2−y+1)dA=36−24+12=24.

First, notice that we have $R={R}_{1}\cup {R}_{2}$, where ${R}_{1}=(-1,1)\times (0,\pi )$ and ${R}_{2}=(1,2)\times (0,\pi ).$ So, we can write

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A= & ={∬}_{{R}_{1}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{{R}_{2}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{{R}_{1}}\operatorname{cos}⁡y\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{{R}_{2}}x\operatorname{sin}⁡y\,\text{d}A \\  & =(1-(-1)){\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡y\,\text{d}y+({\int }_{1}^{2}x\,\text{d}x)({\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡y\,\text{d}y) \\  & =2[\operatorname{sin}⁡y]_{0}^{\pi }+[\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}]_{1}^{2}\cdot [-\operatorname{cos}⁡y]_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =2(0)+(2-\frac{1}{2})\cdot (-(-1)+1) \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

judgments.reasoning: Additivity over S, T, and U gives the sum of their integrals, with the U contribution zero. The earlier answer, option d, was graded Correct and matches the final expression in Math Academy's worked solution.

The two rectangles contribute 1 and e²−e, giving 1+e²−e, option c, as previously solved and as Math Academy's solution states. The recorded submission was option a, so its Incorrect grade is consistent. The worked solution contains a differential typo: the integral of 3x² should use dx, not dy; its final answer is correct.
Linearity gives 36−24+12=24. The earlier answer and recorded submission, option c, were graded Correct and agree with Math Academy's worked solution.

The first rectangle contributes 2[sin(y)]₀^π=0; the second contributes [x²/2]₁²[−cos(y)]₀^π=(3/2)(2)=3. This confirms the earlier answer, option d, and agrees with Math Academy's worked solution. The recorded submission was option a, 5/2, so its Incorrect grade is consistent.

Linearity and additivity give (1/3)(2+7)=3, confirming the earlier answer, option b. The submitted value 3 was graded Correct and matches the worked solution's final answer. The solution incorrectly writes 5f in its opening integral; that integrand would give 45 and should instead be (1/3)f.

Question 1
?

Consider the region R shown above. Let the function f(x,y) be defined as f(x,y)={ex,(x,y)∈S,x2+y,(x,y)∈T,0,(x,y)∈U. Then, ∬Rf(x,y) dA=

a
∬SexdA+∬TxdA+∬U(x2+y)dA
b
∬SexdA+∬T(x2+y)dA+∬UxdA
c
∬S(x2+y)dA+∬TexdA+∬UdA
d
∬SexdA+∬T(x2+y)dA
e
∬SyexdA+∬Tx2dA+∬UdA
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, notice that the domain R can be represented as a union of three sub-domains, as follows:

R=S∪T∪U.

So, we can write

Question 1
?

Consider the region R shown above. Let the function f(x,y) be defined as f(x,y)={ex,(x,y)∈S,x2+y,(x,y)∈T,0,(x,y)∈U. Then, ∬Rf(x,y) dA=

a
∬SexdA+∬TxdA+∬U(x2+y)dA
b
∬SexdA+∬T(x2+y)dA+∬UxdA
c
∬S(x2+y)dA+∬TexdA+∬UdA
d
∬SexdA+∬T(x2+y)dA
e
∬SyexdA+∬Tx2dA+∬UdA
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, notice that the domain R can be represented as a union of three sub-domains, as follows:

R=S∪T∪U.

So, we can write

∬Rf(x,y)dA=∬Sf(x,y)dA+∬Tf(x,y)dA+∬Uf(x,y)dA=∬SexdA+∬T(x2+y)dA+∬U0dA=∬SexdA+∬T(x2+y)dA.

solution.reasoning: By additivity over the regions S, T, and U, the integral equals the integral of e^x over S plus the integral of x^2+y over T. The integral over U is zero because f=0 there. Thus option d is mathematically correct. No captured Math Academy answer or grade establishes its stated key.

Question 1
?

Consider the region R shown above. Let the function f(x,y) be defined as f(x,y)={ex,(x,y)∈S,x2+y,(x,y)∈T,0,(x,y)∈U. Then, ∬Rf(x,y) dA=

a
∬SexdA+∬TxdA+∬U(x2+y)dA
b
∬SexdA+∬T(x2+y)dA+∬UxdA
c
∬S(x2+y)dA+∬TexdA+∬UdA
d
∬SexdA+∬T(x2+y)dA
e
∬SyexdA+∬Tx2dA+∬UdA
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, notice that the domain R can be represented as a union of three sub-domains, as follows:

R=S∪T∪U.

So, we can write

∬Rf(x,y)dA=∬Sf(x,y)dA+∬Tf(x,y)dA+∬Uf(x,y)dA=∬SexdA+∬T(x2+y)dA+∬U0dA=∬SexdA+∬T(x2+y)dA.

Question 2
?

Evaluate the double integral ∬Rf(x,y)dA, where f(x,y)={3x2,if0<x<1,0<y<1,2x ey,if0<x<1,1<y<2, and R is the domain of f.

a
 1−e2
b
 1+e2+e
c
 1+e2−e
d
 1−e2
e
 1+e2
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, notice that we have R=R1∪R2, where R1=(0,1)×(0,1) and R2=(0,1)×(1,2). So, we can write

First, notice that we have R=R1∪R2, where R1=(0,1)×(0,1) and R2=(0,1)×(1,2). So, we can write

∬Rf(x,y)dA=∬R1f(x,y)dA+∬R2f(x,y)dA=∬R13x2dA+∬R22x eydA=(1−0)∫013x2dy+(∫012xdx)(∫12eydy)=x3|01+(x2|01)⋅(ey|12)=1+1⋅(e2−e1)=1+e2−e.

question.name: Question 3
question.problem: Calculate ${∬}_{R}({x}^{2}-y+1)\,\text{d}A$,  where $R=[-3,0]\times [0,4].$
question.worked_solution:
Using the linearity property of double integrals, we can write

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}({x}^{2}-y+1)\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{R}{x}^{2}\text{ }\text{d}A-{∬}_{R}y\text{ }\text{d}A+{∬}_{R}\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

The function under the first integral is independent of $y.$ So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}{x}^{2}\text{ }\text{d}A & =(4-0){\int }_{-3}^{0}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =4[\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}]_{-3}^{0} \\  & =4(\frac{{0}^{3}}{3}-\frac{(-3)^{3}}{3}) \\  & =36.\end{aligned}
$$

The function under the second integral is independent of $x.$ So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}y\text{ }\text{d}A & =(0-(-3)){\int }_{0}^{4}y\,\text{d}y \\  & =3[\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}]_{0}^{4} \\  & =3(\frac{{4}^{2}}{2}-\frac{{0}^{2}}{2}) \\  & =24.\end{aligned}
$$

The third integral is the double integral of unity:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}\text{d}A=\text{Area}(R)=3\cdot 4=12\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, combining our results, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}({x}^{2}-y+1)\,\text{d}A=36-24+12=24.\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 3
?

Calculate ∬R(x2−y+1)dA, where R=[−3,0]×[0,4].

a
0
b
12
c
24
d
36
e
72
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Using the linearity property of double integrals, we can write

∬R(x2−y+1)dA=∬Rx2 dA−∬Ry dA+∬RdA.

The function under the first integral is independent of y. So, we have

∬Rx2 dA=(4−0)∫−30x2dx=4[x33]−30=4(033−(−3)33)=36.

The function under the second integral is independent of x. So, we have

∬Ry dA=(0−(−3))∫04ydy=3[y22]04=3(422−022)=24.

The third integral is the double integral of unity:

∬RdA=Area(R)=3⋅4=12

Finally, combining our results, we obtain

∬R(x2−y+1)dA=36−24+12=24.

last_observation.name: Question 3
last_observation.worked_solution:
Using the linearity property of double integrals, we can write

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}({x}^{2}-y+1)\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{R}{x}^{2}\text{ }\text{d}A-{∬}_{R}y\text{ }\text{d}A+{∬}_{R}\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

The function under the first integral is independent of $y.$ So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}{x}^{2}\text{ }\text{d}A & =(4-0){\int }_{-3}^{0}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =4[\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}]_{-3}^{0} \\  & =4(\frac{{0}^{3}}{3}-\frac{(-3)^{3}}{3}) \\  & =36.\end{aligned}
$$

The function under the second integral is independent of $x.$ So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}y\text{ }\text{d}A & =(0-(-3)){\int }_{0}^{4}y\,\text{d}y \\  & =3[\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}]_{0}^{4} \\  & =3(\frac{{4}^{2}}{2}-\frac{{0}^{2}}{2}) \\  & =24.\end{aligned}
$$

The third integral is the double integral of unity:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}\text{d}A=\text{Area}(R)=3\cdot 4=12\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, combining our results, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}({x}^{2}-y+1)\,\text{d}A=36-24+12=24.\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 4
question.problem:
Evaluate the double integral ${∬}_{R}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A$, where

$$
f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡y,\, & \text{if}\,-1<x<1,\,0<y<\pi , \\ x\operatorname{sin}⁡y,\, & \text{if}\,1<x<2,\,0<y<\pi ,\end{aligned}
$$

and  $R$ is the domain of $f.$
question.worked_solution:
First, notice that we have $R={R}_{1}\cup {R}_{2}$, where ${R}_{1}=(-1,1)\times (0,\pi )$ and ${R}_{2}=(1,2)\times (0,\pi ).$ So, we can write

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A= & ={∬}_{{R}_{1}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{{R}_{2}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{{R}_{1}}\operatorname{cos}⁡y\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{{R}_{2}}x\operatorname{sin}⁡y\,\text{d}A \\  & =(1-(-1)){\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡y\,\text{d}y+({\int }_{1}^{2}x\,\text{d}x)({\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡y\,\text{d}y) \\  & =2[\operatorname{sin}⁡y]_{0}^{\pi }+[\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}]_{1}^{2}\cdot [-\operatorname{cos}⁡y]_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =2(0)+(2-\frac{1}{2})\cdot (-(-1)+1) \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem:
The region $R$ is enclosed inside the sphere ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}=9$ for $x\ge 0.$
Express the following triple integral in spherical polar coordinates. 

$$
{∭}_{R}\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}V
$$
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,dV={∭}_{Δ}\,f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ)\,{\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ.
$$

If $(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)$ are the spherical coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the following formulas:

$$
x=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,y=\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,z=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ
$$

Notice that the region $R$ represents one-half of the sphere of radius $3$ centered at the origin.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14178392/assets/d2b9c6f3541c47f37ad7f2ba52d739787e39600ec71fe3530f0ad2846c24880b.png)

 

As a result, we obtain that in spherical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ=\{(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)\,:\,0\le \rho \le 3,\,-\frac{\pi }{2}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2},\,0\le ϕ\le \pi \}.
$$

Next, we substitute the spherical polar coordinates into the function $f(x,y,z)=\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ) \\  & =\sqrt{(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ)^{2}+(\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{\rho }^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta {sin}^{2}⁡ϕ+{\rho }^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta {sin}^{2}⁡ϕ} \\  & =\sqrt{{\rho }^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡ϕ({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )} \\  & =\sqrt{{\rho }^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡ϕ} \\  & =\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain  

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}V & ={∭}_{Δ}\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\cdot {\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{3}{\rho }^{3}{sin}^{2}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 2
questions.problem:
The region $R$ is enclosed inside the sphere ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}=3.$
Express the following triple integral in spherical polar coordinates. 

$$
{∭}_{R}{y}^{2}\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}\,\text{d}V
$$
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,dV={∭}_{Δ}\,f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ)\,{\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ.
$$

If $(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)$ are the spherical coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the following formulas:

$$
x=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,y=\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,z=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ
$$

Notice that the region $R$ represents the sphere of radius $\sqrt{3}$ centered at the origin. 
As a result, in spherical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ=\{(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)\,:\,0\le \rho \le \sqrt{3},\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi ,\,0\le ϕ\le \pi \}.
$$

Next, we substitute the spherical polar coordinates into the function $f(x,y,z)={y}^{2}\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ) \\  & =(\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ)^{2}\cdot \rho  \\  & ={\rho }^{3}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta {sin}^{2}⁡ϕ\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain  

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}{y}^{2}\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}\,\text{d}V & ={∭}_{Δ}{\rho }^{3}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta {sin}^{2}⁡ϕ\cdot {\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3}}{\rho }^{5}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta {sin}^{3}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 3
questions.problem:
Evaluate the triple integral

$$
{∭}_{R}{z}^{2}\,\text{d}V
$$

over the region $R$ enclosed inside the sphere ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}=4.$
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,dV={∭}_{Δ}\,f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ)\,{\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ.
$$

If $(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)$ are the spherical coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the following formulas:

$$
x=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,y=\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,z=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ
$$

Notice that the region $R$ represents the sphere of radius $2$ centered at the origin. 
As a result, in spherical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ=\{(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)\,:\,0\le \rho \le 2,\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi ,\,0\le ϕ\le \pi \}.
$$

Next, we substitute the spherical polar coordinates into the function $f(x,y,z)={z}^{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ) \\  & =(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ) \\  & ={\rho }^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡ϕ\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}z\,\text{d}V & ={∭}_{Δ}{\rho }^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡ϕ\cdot {\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{2}{\rho }^{4}{cos}^{2}⁡ϕ\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{cos}^{2}⁡ϕ\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,dϕ\cdot {\int }_{0}^{2\pi }d\theta \cdot {\int }_{0}^{2}{\rho }^{4}\,d\rho  \\  & ={[-\frac{1}{3}{cos}^{3}⁡ϕ]}_{ϕ=0}^{ϕ=\pi }\cdot [\theta ]_{\theta =0}^{\theta =2\pi }\cdot {[\frac{1}{5}{\rho }^{5}]}_{\rho =0}^{\rho =2}\,d\rho  \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}(-1-1)\cdot (2\pi -0)\cdot \frac{1}{5}(32-0) \\  & =\frac{2}{3}\cdot 2\pi \cdot \frac{32}{5} \\  & =\frac{128\pi }{15}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 4
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14178392/assets/2fd023af7c229d813344ee366b384a5917b69df0d06fabff6466b9ebcc199bb9.png)

Evaluate the triple integral

$$
{∭}_{R}{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2})}^{2}\,\text{d}V
$$

over the region $R$ enclosed inside the sphere ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}=4$ for $y\le 0$ and $z\le 0,$ shown above.
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,dV={∭}_{Δ}\,f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ)\,{\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ.
$$

If $(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)$ are the spherical coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the following formulas:

$$
x=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,y=\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,z=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ
$$

Notice that the region $R$ represents one-quarter of the sphere of radius $2$ centered at the origin.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14178392/assets/090f210768ffd4a6be529860b54a2906e265427b7d85bcbb07e3101c801740ba.png)

 

As a result, we obtain that in spherical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ=\{(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)\,:\,0\le \rho \le 2,\,\pi \le \theta \le 2\pi ,\,\frac{\pi }{2}\le ϕ\le \pi \}.
$$

Next, we substitute the spherical polar coordinates into the function $f(x,y,z)={({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2})}^{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ) \\  & ={({\rho }^{2})}^{2} \\  & ={\rho }^{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2})}^{2}\,\text{d}V & ={∭}_{Δ}{\rho }^{4}\cdot {\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }{\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{2}{\rho }^{6}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,dϕ\cdot {\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }d\theta \cdot {\int }_{0}^{2}{\rho }^{6}\,d\rho  \\  & =[-\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ]_{ϕ=\pi /2}^{ϕ=\pi }\cdot [\theta ]_{\theta =\pi }^{\theta =2\pi }\cdot {[\frac{1}{7}{\rho }^{7}]}_{\rho =0}^{\rho =2} \\  & =-(-1-0)\cdot (2\pi -\pi )\cdot \frac{1}{7}(128-0) \\  & =1\cdot \pi \cdot \frac{128}{7} \\  & =\frac{128\pi }{7}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 5
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14178392/assets/4d2a71ffdce7f02cdfa78881c7e355c9aada4134cf06b663a2deefb3d779b9ca.png)

The region $R$ is enclosed inside the sphere ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}=8x,$ shown above. 
Express the following triple integral in spherical polar coordinates. 

$$
{∭}_{R}y\,\text{d}V
$$
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,dV={∭}_{Δ}\,f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ)\,{\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ.
$$

If $(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)$ are the spherical coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the following formulas:

$$
x=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,y=\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,z=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ
$$

Notice that the region $R$ represents the sphere of radius $4$ centered at $(4,0,0).$

With that in mind, let's now write the ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}=8x$ in spherical polar coordinates:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2} & =8x \\ {\rho }^{2} & =8\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ \\ \rho (\rho -8\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

 

Since $\rho $ cannot be identical to zero on the entire sphere, we must have $\rho =8\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14178392/assets/0475e2e272a30318dc4cb31457539a312544b6e14d7e6a8ed3f911d41404b575.png)

 

As a result, we obtain that in spherical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ=\{(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)\,:\,0\le \rho \le 8\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,-\frac{\pi }{2}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2},\,0\le ϕ\le \pi \}.
$$

Next, we substitute the spherical polar coordinates into the function $f(x,y,z)=y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ) \\  & =\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain  

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}y\,\text{d}V & ={∭}_{Δ}\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\cdot {\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{8\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ}{\rho }^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {sin}^{2}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.raw_html:
5.Rewriting a Triple Integral Defined Over a Shifted Sphere ?

The region R is enclosed inside the sphere x2+y2+z2=8x, shown above. Express the following triple integral in spherical polar coordinates. ∭RydV

M
Tue, Oct 13th @ 10:47 AM|Elapsed: 0:18Correct

observed_steps.name: Question 1
observed_steps.worked_solution:
We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,dV={∭}_{Δ}\,f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ)\,{\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ.
$$

If $(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)$ are the spherical coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the following formulas:

$$
x=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,y=\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,z=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ
$$

Notice that the region $R$ represents one-half of the sphere of radius $3$ centered at the origin.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14178392/assets/d2b9c6f3541c47f37ad7f2ba52d739787e39600ec71fe3530f0ad2846c24880b.png)

 

As a result, we obtain that in spherical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ=\{(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)\,:\,0\le \rho \le 3,\,-\frac{\pi }{2}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2},\,0\le ϕ\le \pi \}.
$$

Next, we substitute the spherical polar coordinates into the function $f(x,y,z)=\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ) \\  & =\sqrt{(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ)^{2}+(\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{\rho }^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta {sin}^{2}⁡ϕ+{\rho }^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta {sin}^{2}⁡ϕ} \\  & =\sqrt{{\rho }^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡ϕ({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )} \\  & =\sqrt{{\rho }^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡ϕ} \\  & =\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain  

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}V & ={∭}_{Δ}\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\cdot {\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{3}{\rho }^{3}{sin}^{2}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 1
?

The region R is enclosed inside the sphere x2+y2+z2=9 for x≥0. Express the following triple integral in spherical polar coordinates. ∭Rx2+y2dV

a
 ∫0π∫0π∫03ρ3cos⁡ϕdρdθdϕ
b
 ∫0π∫0π∫03ρ3cos⁡ϕsin2⁡ϕdρdθdϕ
c
∫0π∫−π/2π/2∫03ρ3sin2⁡ϕdρdθdϕ
d
 ∫0π∫0π/2∫03ρ3sin2⁡ϕdρdθdϕ
e
 ∫0π∫−π/2π/2∫03ρ3cos⁡ϕdρdθdϕ
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

We will use the change of variables formula in the form

∭Rf(x,y,z)dV=∭Δf(ρcos⁡θsin⁡ϕ,ρsin⁡θsin⁡ϕ,ρcos⁡ϕ)ρ2sin⁡ϕdρdθdϕ.

If (ρ,θ,ϕ) are the spherical coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates (x,y,z) can be found by using the following formulas:

x=ρcos⁡θsin⁡ϕ,y=ρsin⁡θsin⁡ϕ,z=ρcos⁡ϕ

Notice that the region R represents one-half of the sphere of radius 3 centered at the origin.

As a result, we obtain that in spherical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as

Δ={(ρ,θ,ϕ):0≤ρ≤3,−π2≤θ≤π2,0≤ϕ≤π}.

Next, we substitute the spherical polar coordinates into the function f(x,y,z)=x2+y2:

f(x,y,z)=f(ρcos⁡θsin⁡ϕ,ρsin⁡θsin⁡ϕ,ρcos⁡ϕ)=(ρcos⁡θsin⁡ϕ)2+(ρsin⁡θsin⁡ϕ)2=ρ2cos2⁡θsin2⁡ϕ+ρ2sin2⁡θsin2⁡ϕ=ρ2sin2⁡ϕ(cos2⁡θ+sin2⁡θ)=ρ2sin2⁡ϕ=ρsin⁡ϕ

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain

∭Rx2+y2dV=∭Δρsin⁡ϕ⋅ρ2sin⁡ϕdρdθdϕ=∫0π∫−π/2π/2∫03ρ3sin2⁡ϕdρdθdϕ.

observed_steps.name: Question 2
observed_steps.worked_solution:
We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,dV={∭}_{Δ}\,f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ)\,{\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ.
$$

If $(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)$ are the spherical coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the following formulas:

$$
x=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,y=\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,z=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ
$$

Notice that the region $R$ represents the sphere of radius $\sqrt{3}$ centered at the origin. 
As a result, in spherical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ=\{(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)\,:\,0\le \rho \le \sqrt{3},\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi ,\,0\le ϕ\le \pi \}.
$$

Next, we substitute the spherical polar coordinates into the function $f(x,y,z)={y}^{2}\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ) \\  & =(\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ)^{2}\cdot \rho  \\  & ={\rho }^{3}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta {sin}^{2}⁡ϕ\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain  

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}{y}^{2}\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}\,\text{d}V & ={∭}_{Δ}{\rho }^{3}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta {sin}^{2}⁡ϕ\cdot {\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3}}{\rho }^{5}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta {sin}^{3}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ.\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 2
question.problem:
The region $R$ is enclosed inside the sphere ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}=3.$
Express the following triple integral in spherical polar coordinates. 

$$
{∭}_{R}{y}^{2}\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}\,\text{d}V
$$

Question 2
?

The region R is enclosed inside the sphere x2+y2+z2=3. Express the following triple integral in spherical polar coordinates. ∭Ry2x2+y2+z2dV

a
∫02π∫02π∫03ρ4cos2⁡ϕsin2⁡ϕdρdθdϕ
b
∫02π∫02π∫03ρ5cos2⁡θsin3⁡ϕdρdθdϕ
c
∫0π∫02π∫03ρ5sin2⁡θsin3⁡ϕdρdθdϕ
d
∫0π∫02π∫03ρ4sin⁡θsin2⁡ϕdρdθdϕ
e
∫0π∫02π∫03ρ5cos2⁡θsin⁡θsin⁡ϕdρdθdϕ
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We will use the change of variables formula in the form

∭Rf(x,y,z)dV=∭Δf(ρcos⁡θsin⁡ϕ,ρsin⁡θsin⁡ϕ,ρcos⁡ϕ)ρ2sin⁡ϕdρdθdϕ.

If (ρ,θ,ϕ) are the spherical coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates (x,y,z) can be found by using the following formulas:

x=ρcos⁡θsin⁡ϕ,y=ρsin⁡θsin⁡ϕ,z=ρcos⁡ϕ

Notice that the region R represents the sphere of radius 3 centered at the origin. As a result, in spherical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as

Δ={(ρ,θ,ϕ):0≤ρ≤3,0≤θ≤2π,0≤ϕ≤π}.

Next, we substitute the spherical polar coordinates into the function f(x,y,z)=y2x2+y2+z2:

f(x,y,z)=f(ρcos⁡θsin⁡ϕ,ρsin⁡θsin⁡ϕ,ρcos⁡ϕ)=(ρsin⁡θsin⁡ϕ)2⋅ρ=ρ3sin2⁡θsin2⁡ϕ

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain

∭Ry2x2+y2+z2dV=∭Δρ3sin2⁡θsin2⁡ϕ⋅ρ2sin⁡ϕdρdθdϕ=∫0π∫02π∫03ρ5sin2⁡θsin3⁡ϕdρdθdϕ.

observed_steps.name: Question 3
observed_steps.worked_solution:
We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,dV={∭}_{Δ}\,f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ)\,{\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ.
$$

If $(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)$ are the spherical coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the following formulas:

$$
x=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,y=\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,z=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ
$$

Notice that the region $R$ represents the sphere of radius $2$ centered at the origin. 
As a result, in spherical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ=\{(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)\,:\,0\le \rho \le 2,\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi ,\,0\le ϕ\le \pi \}.
$$

Next, we substitute the spherical polar coordinates into the function $f(x,y,z)={z}^{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ) \\  & =(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ) \\  & ={\rho }^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡ϕ\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}z\,\text{d}V & ={∭}_{Δ}{\rho }^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡ϕ\cdot {\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{2}{\rho }^{4}{cos}^{2}⁡ϕ\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{cos}^{2}⁡ϕ\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,dϕ\cdot {\int }_{0}^{2\pi }d\theta \cdot {\int }_{0}^{2}{\rho }^{4}\,d\rho  \\  & ={[-\frac{1}{3}{cos}^{3}⁡ϕ]}_{ϕ=0}^{ϕ=\pi }\cdot [\theta ]_{\theta =0}^{\theta =2\pi }\cdot {[\frac{1}{5}{\rho }^{5}]}_{\rho =0}^{\rho =2}\,d\rho  \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}(-1-1)\cdot (2\pi -0)\cdot \frac{1}{5}(32-0) \\  & =\frac{2}{3}\cdot 2\pi \cdot \frac{32}{5} \\  & =\frac{128\pi }{15}\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

Next, we substitute the spherical polar coordinates into the function $f(x,y,z)={({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2})}^{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ) \\  & ={({\rho }^{2})}^{2} \\  & ={\rho }^{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2})}^{2}\,\text{d}V & ={∭}_{Δ}{\rho }^{4}\cdot {\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }{\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{2}{\rho }^{6}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,dϕ\cdot {\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }d\theta \cdot {\int }_{0}^{2}{\rho }^{6}\,d\rho  \\  & =[-\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ]_{ϕ=\pi /2}^{ϕ=\pi }\cdot [\theta ]_{\theta =\pi }^{\theta =2\pi }\cdot {[\frac{1}{7}{\rho }^{7}]}_{\rho =0}^{\rho =2} \\  & =-(-1-0)\cdot (2\pi -\pi )\cdot \frac{1}{7}(128-0) \\  & =1\cdot \pi \cdot \frac{128}{7} \\  & =\frac{128\pi }{7}\end{aligned}
$$

?

Evaluate the triple integral ∭R(x2+y2+z2)2dV over the region R enclosed inside the sphere x2+y2+z2=4 for y≤0 and z≤0, shown above.

a
128π7

EXPLANATION

We will use the change of variables formula in the form ∭Rf(x,y,z)dV=∭Δf(ρcos⁡θsin⁡ϕ,ρsin⁡θsin⁡ϕ,ρcos⁡ϕ)ρ2sin⁡ϕdρdθdϕ.

If (ρ,θ,ϕ) are the spherical coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates (x,y,z) can be found by using the following formulas: x=ρcos⁡θsin⁡ϕ,y=ρsin⁡θsin⁡ϕ,z=ρcos⁡ϕ

Notice that the region R represents one-quarter of the sphere of radius 2 centered at the origin.

As a result, we obtain that in spherical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as

Δ={(ρ,θ,ϕ):0≤ρ≤2,π≤θ≤2π,π2≤ϕ≤π}.

Next, we substitute the spherical polar coordinates into the function f(x,y,z)=(x2+y2+z2)2: f(x,y,z)=f(ρcos⁡θsin⁡ϕ,ρsin⁡θsin⁡ϕ,ρcos⁡ϕ)=(ρ2)2=ρ4

∭R(x2+y2+z2)2dV=∭Δρ4⋅ρ2sin⁡ϕdρdθdϕ=∫π/2π∫π2π∫02ρ6sin⁡ϕdρdθdϕ=∫π/2πsin⁡ϕdϕ⋅∫π2πdθ⋅∫02ρ6dρ=[−cos⁡ϕ]ϕ=π/2ϕ=π⋅[θ]θ=πθ=2π⋅[17ρ7]ρ=0ρ=2=−(−1−0)⋅(2π−π)⋅17(128−0)=1⋅π⋅1287=128π7

observed_steps.worked_solution:
We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,dV={∭}_{Δ}\,f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ)\,{\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ.
$$

If $(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)$ are the spherical coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the following formulas:

$$
x=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,y=\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,z=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ
$$

Notice that the region $R$ represents the sphere of radius $4$ centered at $(4,0,0).$

With that in mind, let's now write the ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}=8x$ in spherical polar coordinates:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2} & =8x \\ {\rho }^{2} & =8\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ \\ \rho (\rho -8\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

 

Since $\rho $ cannot be identical to zero on the entire sphere, we must have $\rho =8\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14178392/assets/0475e2e272a30318dc4cb31457539a312544b6e14d7e6a8ed3f911d41404b575.png)

 

As a result, we obtain that in spherical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ=\{(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)\,:\,0\le \rho \le 8\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,-\frac{\pi }{2}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2},\,0\le ϕ\le \pi \}.
$$

Next, we substitute the spherical polar coordinates into the function $f(x,y,z)=y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ) \\  & =\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain  

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}y\,\text{d}V & ={∭}_{Δ}\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\cdot {\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{8\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ}{\rho }^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {sin}^{2}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 5
?

The region R is enclosed inside the sphere x2+y2+z2=8x, shown above. Express the following triple integral in spherical polar coordinates. ∭RydV

a
 ∫0π∫−π/2π/2∫08cos⁡θsin⁡ϕρ3sin⁡θsin2⁡ϕdρdθdϕ
b
 ∫0π∫−π/2π/2∫04sin⁡ϕρ3sin3⁡ϕdρdθdϕ
c
 ∫0π∫0π/2∫04sin⁡ϕρ3sin⁡θsin2⁡ϕdρdθdϕ v
d
 ∫0π∫−π/2π/2∫08cos⁡θsin⁡ϕρ3sin3⁡ϕdρdθdϕ
e
 ∫0π∫0π/2∫08cos⁡θsin⁡ϕρ3cos⁡θsin2⁡ϕdρdθdϕ v
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We will use the change of variables formula in the form

∭Rf(x,y,z)dV=∭Δf(ρcos⁡θsin⁡ϕ,ρsin⁡θsin⁡ϕ,ρcos⁡ϕ)ρ2sin⁡ϕdρdθdϕ.

If (ρ,θ,ϕ) are the spherical coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates (x,y,z) can be found by using the following formulas:

x=ρcos⁡θsin⁡ϕ,y=ρsin⁡θsin⁡ϕ,z=ρcos⁡ϕ

Notice that the region R represents the sphere of radius 4 centered at (4,0,0).

With that in mind, let's now write the x2+y2+z2=8x in spherical polar coordinates:

x2+y2+z2=8xρ2=8ρcos⁡θsin⁡ϕρ(ρ−8cos⁡θsin⁡ϕ)=0

Since ρ cannot be identical to zero on the entire sphere, we must have ρ=8cos⁡θsin⁡ϕ.

As a result, we obtain that in spherical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as

Δ={(ρ,θ,ϕ):0≤ρ≤8cos⁡θsin⁡ϕ,−π2≤θ≤π2,0≤ϕ≤π}.

Next, we substitute the spherical polar coordinates into the function f(x,y,z)=y:

f(x,y,z)=f(ρcos⁡θsin⁡ϕ,ρsin⁡θsin⁡ϕ,ρcos⁡ϕ)=ρsin⁡θsin⁡ϕ

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain

∭RydV=∭Δρsin⁡θsin⁡ϕ⋅ρ2sin⁡ϕdρdθdϕ=∫0π∫−π/2π/2∫08cos⁡θsin⁡ϕρ3sin⁡θsin2⁡ϕdρdθdϕ.

question.name: Question 1
question.problem:
The region $R$ is enclosed inside the sphere ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}=9$ for $x\ge 0.$
Express the following triple integral in spherical polar coordinates. 

$$
{∭}_{R}\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}V
$$
question.worked_solution:
We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,dV={∭}_{Δ}\,f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ)\,{\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ.
$$

If $(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)$ are the spherical coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the following formulas:

$$
x=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,y=\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,z=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ
$$

Notice that the region $R$ represents one-half of the sphere of radius $3$ centered at the origin.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14178392/assets/d2b9c6f3541c47f37ad7f2ba52d739787e39600ec71fe3530f0ad2846c24880b.png)

 

As a result, we obtain that in spherical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ=\{(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)\,:\,0\le \rho \le 3,\,-\frac{\pi }{2}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2},\,0\le ϕ\le \pi \}.
$$

Next, we substitute the spherical polar coordinates into the function $f(x,y,z)=\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ) \\  & =\sqrt{(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ)^{2}+(\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{\rho }^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta {sin}^{2}⁡ϕ+{\rho }^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta {sin}^{2}⁡ϕ} \\  & =\sqrt{{\rho }^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡ϕ({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )} \\  & =\sqrt{{\rho }^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡ϕ} \\  & =\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain  

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}V & ={∭}_{Δ}\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\cdot {\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{3}{\rho }^{3}{sin}^{2}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 1
?

The region R is enclosed inside the sphere x2+y2+z2=9 for x≥0. Express the following triple integral in spherical polar coordinates. ∭Rx2+y2dV

a
 ∫0π∫0π∫03ρ3cos⁡ϕdρdθdϕ
b
 ∫0π∫0π∫03ρ3cos⁡ϕsin2⁡ϕdρdθdϕ
c
∫0π∫−π/2π/2∫03ρ3sin2⁡ϕdρdθdϕ
d
 ∫0π∫0π/2∫03ρ3sin2⁡ϕdρdθdϕ
e
 ∫0π∫−π/2π/2∫03ρ3cos⁡ϕdρdθdϕ
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

We will use the change of variables formula in the form

∭Rf(x,y,z)dV=∭Δf(ρcos⁡θsin⁡ϕ,ρsin⁡θsin⁡ϕ,ρcos⁡ϕ)ρ2sin⁡ϕdρdθdϕ.

If (ρ,θ,ϕ) are the spherical coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates (x,y,z) can be found by using the following formulas:

x=ρcos⁡θsin⁡ϕ,y=ρsin⁡θsin⁡ϕ,z=ρcos⁡ϕ

Notice that the region R represents one-half of the sphere of radius 3 centered at the origin.

As a result, we obtain that in spherical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as

Δ={(ρ,θ,ϕ):0≤ρ≤3,−π2≤θ≤π2,0≤ϕ≤π}.

Next, we substitute the spherical polar coordinates into the function f(x,y,z)=x2+y2:

f(x,y,z)=f(ρcos⁡θsin⁡ϕ,ρsin⁡θsin⁡ϕ,ρcos⁡ϕ)=(ρcos⁡θsin⁡ϕ)2+(ρsin⁡θsin⁡ϕ)2=ρ2cos2⁡θsin2⁡ϕ+ρ2sin2⁡θsin2⁡ϕ=ρ2sin2⁡ϕ(cos2⁡θ+sin2⁡θ)=ρ2sin2⁡ϕ=ρsin⁡ϕ

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain

∭Rx2+y2dV=∭Δρsin⁡ϕ⋅ρ2sin⁡ϕdρdθdϕ=∫0π∫−π/2π/2∫03ρ3sin2⁡ϕdρdθdϕ.

last_observation.name: Question 1
last_observation.worked_solution:
We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,dV={∭}_{Δ}\,f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ)\,{\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ.
$$

If $(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)$ are the spherical coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the following formulas:

$$
x=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,y=\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,z=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ
$$

Notice that the region $R$ represents one-half of the sphere of radius $3$ centered at the origin.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14178392/assets/d2b9c6f3541c47f37ad7f2ba52d739787e39600ec71fe3530f0ad2846c24880b.png)

 

As a result, we obtain that in spherical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ=\{(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)\,:\,0\le \rho \le 3,\,-\frac{\pi }{2}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2},\,0\le ϕ\le \pi \}.
$$

Next, we substitute the spherical polar coordinates into the function $f(x,y,z)=\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ) \\  & =\sqrt{(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ)^{2}+(\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{\rho }^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta {sin}^{2}⁡ϕ+{\rho }^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta {sin}^{2}⁡ϕ} \\  & =\sqrt{{\rho }^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡ϕ({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )} \\  & =\sqrt{{\rho }^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡ϕ} \\  & =\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain  

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}V & ={∭}_{Δ}\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\cdot {\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{3}{\rho }^{3}{sin}^{2}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

question.html:
Question 1
?

The region R is enclosed inside the sphere x2+y2+z2=9 for x≥0. Express the following triple integral in spherical polar coordinates. ∭Rx2+y2dV

a
 ∫0π∫0π∫03ρ3cos⁡ϕdρdθdϕ
b
 ∫0π∫0π∫03ρ3cos⁡ϕsin2⁡ϕdρdθdϕ
c
∫0π∫−π/2π/2∫03ρ3sin2⁡ϕdρdθdϕ
d
 ∫0π∫0π/2∫03ρ3sin2⁡ϕdρdθdϕ
e
 ∫0π∫−π/2π/2∫03ρ3cos⁡ϕdρdθdϕ
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

We will use the change of variables formula in the form

∭Rf(x,y,z)dV=∭Δf(ρcos⁡θsin⁡ϕ,ρsin⁡θsin⁡ϕ,ρcos⁡ϕ)ρ2sin⁡ϕdρdθdϕ.

If (ρ,θ,ϕ) are the spherical coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates (x,y,z) can be found by using the following formulas:

x=ρcos⁡θsin⁡ϕ,y=ρsin⁡θsin⁡ϕ,z=ρcos⁡ϕ

Notice that the region R represents one-half of the sphere of radius 3 centered at the origin.

As a result, we obtain that in spherical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as

Δ={(ρ,θ,ϕ):0≤ρ≤3,−π2≤θ≤π2,0≤ϕ≤π}.

Next, we substitute the spherical polar coordinates into the function f(x,y,z)=x2+y2:

f(x,y,z)=f(ρcos⁡θsin⁡ϕ,ρsin⁡θsin⁡ϕ,ρcos⁡ϕ)=(ρcos⁡θsin⁡ϕ)2+(ρsin⁡θsin⁡ϕ)2=ρ2cos2⁡θsin2⁡ϕ+ρ2sin2⁡θsin2⁡ϕ=ρ2sin2⁡ϕ(cos2⁡θ+sin2⁡θ)=ρ2sin2⁡ϕ=ρsin⁡ϕ

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain

∭Rx2+y2dV=∭Δρsin⁡ϕ⋅ρ2sin⁡ϕdρdθdϕ=∫0π∫−π/2π/2∫03ρ3sin2⁡ϕdρdθdϕ.

solution.reasoning: Using x=\rho\sin\phi\cos\theta, y=\rho\sin\phi\sin\theta, and z=\rho\cos\phi, the integrand becomes \rho\sin\phi and the volume element is \rho^2\sin\phi\,d\rho\,d\theta\,d\phi. Their product is \rho^3\sin^2\phi. The sphere gives 0≤\rho≤3, while x≥0 gives -\pi/2≤\theta≤\pi/2; the polar angle spans 0≤\phi≤\pi. Thus option c is mathematically correct. feedback.problem:
The region $R$ is enclosed inside the sphere ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}=9$ for $x\ge 0.$
Express the following triple integral in spherical polar coordinates. 

$$
{∭}_{R}\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}V
$$
feedback.worked_solution:
We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,dV={∭}_{Δ}\,f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ)\,{\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ.
$$

If $(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)$ are the spherical coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the following formulas:

$$
x=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,y=\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,z=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ
$$

Notice that the region $R$ represents one-half of the sphere of radius $3$ centered at the origin.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14178392/assets/d2b9c6f3541c47f37ad7f2ba52d739787e39600ec71fe3530f0ad2846c24880b.png)

 

As a result, we obtain that in spherical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ=\{(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)\,:\,0\le \rho \le 3,\,-\frac{\pi }{2}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2},\,0\le ϕ\le \pi \}.
$$

Next, we substitute the spherical polar coordinates into the function $f(x,y,z)=\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ) \\  & =\sqrt{(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ)^{2}+(\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{\rho }^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta {sin}^{2}⁡ϕ+{\rho }^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta {sin}^{2}⁡ϕ} \\  & =\sqrt{{\rho }^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡ϕ({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )} \\  & =\sqrt{{\rho }^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡ϕ} \\  & =\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain  

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}V & ={∭}_{Δ}\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\cdot {\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{3}{\rho }^{3}{sin}^{2}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 1

The region R is enclosed inside the sphere x2+y2+z2=9 for x≥0. Express the following triple integral in spherical polar coordinates. ∭Rx2+y2dV

a
 ∫0π∫0π∫03ρ3cos⁡ϕdρdθdϕ
b
 ∫0π∫0π∫03ρ3cos⁡ϕsin2⁡ϕdρdθdϕ
c
∫0π∫−π/2π/2∫03ρ3sin2⁡ϕdρdθdϕ
d
 ∫0π∫0π/2∫03ρ3sin2⁡ϕdρdθdϕ
e
 ∫0π∫−π/2π/2∫03ρ3cos⁡ϕdρdθdϕ
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

We will use the change of variables formula in the form

∭Rf(x,y,z)dV=∭Δf(ρcos⁡θsin⁡ϕ,ρsin⁡θsin⁡ϕ,ρcos⁡ϕ)ρ2sin⁡ϕdρdθdϕ.

If (ρ,θ,ϕ) are the spherical coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates (x,y,z) can be found by using the following formulas:

x=ρcos⁡θsin⁡ϕ,y=ρsin⁡θsin⁡ϕ,z=ρcos⁡ϕ

Notice that the region R represents one-half of the sphere of radius 3 centered at the origin.

As a result, we obtain that in spherical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as

Δ={(ρ,θ,ϕ):0≤ρ≤3,−π2≤θ≤π2,0≤ϕ≤π}.

Next, we substitute the spherical polar coordinates into the function f(x,y,z)=x2+y2:

f(x,y,z)=f(ρcos⁡θsin⁡ϕ,ρsin⁡θsin⁡ϕ,ρcos⁡ϕ)=(ρcos⁡θsin⁡ϕ)2+(ρsin⁡θsin⁡ϕ)2=ρ2cos2⁡θsin2⁡ϕ+ρ2sin2⁡θsin2⁡ϕ=ρ2sin2⁡ϕ(cos2⁡θ+sin2⁡θ)=ρ2sin2⁡ϕ=ρsin⁡ϕ

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain

∭Rx2+y2dV=∭Δρsin⁡ϕ⋅ρ2sin⁡ϕdρdθdϕ=∫0π∫−π/2π/2∫03ρ3sin2⁡ϕdρdθdϕ.

question.name: Question 2
question.problem:
The region $R$ is enclosed inside the sphere ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}=3.$
Express the following triple integral in spherical polar coordinates. 

$$
{∭}_{R}{y}^{2}\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}\,\text{d}V
$$
question.worked_solution:
We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,dV={∭}_{Δ}\,f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ)\,{\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ.
$$

If $(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)$ are the spherical coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the following formulas:

$$
x=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,y=\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,z=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ
$$

Notice that the region $R$ represents the sphere of radius $\sqrt{3}$ centered at the origin. 
As a result, in spherical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ=\{(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)\,:\,0\le \rho \le \sqrt{3},\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi ,\,0\le ϕ\le \pi \}.
$$

Next, we substitute the spherical polar coordinates into the function $f(x,y,z)={y}^{2}\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ) \\  & =(\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ)^{2}\cdot \rho  \\  & ={\rho }^{3}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta {sin}^{2}⁡ϕ\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain  

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}{y}^{2}\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}\,\text{d}V & ={∭}_{Δ}{\rho }^{3}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta {sin}^{2}⁡ϕ\cdot {\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3}}{\rho }^{5}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta {sin}^{3}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 2
?

The region R is enclosed inside the sphere x2+y2+z2=3. Express the following triple integral in spherical polar coordinates. ∭Ry2x2+y2+z2dV

a
∫02π∫02π∫03ρ4cos2⁡ϕsin2⁡ϕdρdθdϕ
b
∫02π∫02π∫03ρ5cos2⁡θsin3⁡ϕdρdθdϕ
c
∫0π∫02π∫03ρ5sin2⁡θsin3⁡ϕdρdθdϕ
d
∫0π∫02π∫03ρ4sin⁡θsin2⁡ϕdρdθdϕ
e
∫0π∫02π∫03ρ5cos2⁡θsin⁡θsin⁡ϕdρdθdϕ
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We will use the change of variables formula in the form

∭Rf(x,y,z)dV=∭Δf(ρcos⁡θsin⁡ϕ,ρsin⁡θsin⁡ϕ,ρcos⁡ϕ)ρ2sin⁡ϕdρdθdϕ.

If (ρ,θ,ϕ) are the spherical coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates (x,y,z) can be found by using the following formulas:

x=ρcos⁡θsin⁡ϕ,y=ρsin⁡θsin⁡ϕ,z=ρcos⁡ϕ

Notice that the region R represents the sphere of radius 3 centered at the origin. As a result, in spherical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as

Δ={(ρ,θ,ϕ):0≤ρ≤3,0≤θ≤2π,0≤ϕ≤π}.

Next, we substitute the spherical polar coordinates into the function f(x,y,z)=y2x2+y2+z2:

f(x,y,z)=f(ρcos⁡θsin⁡ϕ,ρsin⁡θsin⁡ϕ,ρcos⁡ϕ)=(ρsin⁡θsin⁡ϕ)2⋅ρ=ρ3sin2⁡θsin2⁡ϕ

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain

∭Ry2x2+y2+z2dV=∭Δρ3sin2⁡θsin2⁡ϕ⋅ρ2sin⁡ϕdρdθdϕ=∫0π∫02π∫03ρ5sin2⁡θsin3⁡ϕdρdθdϕ.

last_observation.name: Question 2
last_observation.worked_solution:
We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,dV={∭}_{Δ}\,f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ)\,{\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ.
$$

If $(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)$ are the spherical coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the following formulas:

$$
x=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,y=\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,z=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ
$$

Notice that the region $R$ represents the sphere of radius $\sqrt{3}$ centered at the origin. 
As a result, in spherical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ=\{(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)\,:\,0\le \rho \le \sqrt{3},\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi ,\,0\le ϕ\le \pi \}.
$$

Next, we substitute the spherical polar coordinates into the function $f(x,y,z)={y}^{2}\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ) \\  & =(\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ)^{2}\cdot \rho  \\  & ={\rho }^{3}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta {sin}^{2}⁡ϕ\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain  

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}{y}^{2}\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}\,\text{d}V & ={∭}_{Δ}{\rho }^{3}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta {sin}^{2}⁡ϕ\cdot {\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3}}{\rho }^{5}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta {sin}^{3}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ.\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 2
question.problem:
The region $R$ is enclosed inside the sphere ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}=3.$
Express the following triple integral in spherical polar coordinates. 

$$
{∭}_{R}{y}^{2}\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}\,\text{d}V
$$
